speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head S of the Estimates to be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: When it was reported in January this year that China's population declined for the first time since 1961, the Chinese stock markets wobbled.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It was widely expected because of its ageing population and declining fertility.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A reality of potential shrinking consumption and most certainly, a declining workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It faces perhaps a Japanese-style three decades-long economic stagnation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is projected to reach 2.7 in 2030.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A significant number of these 400,000 would have retired by the end of this decade.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These are much higher than that in other industries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But what does this really mean for us as a nation?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our economy would become less vibrant as our workforce shrinks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We might face a hollowing out of certain industries such as in land transport, F&B, tradesman and machine operators.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is less of a problem if it was a gradual shift with sufficient time to adjust.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The oldest of our baby boomer generation is 77 years old and the youngest is 59 years old.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They are likely to exit the workforce by the end of this decade in large numbers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While our birth rate peaked in the late-1970s to the early-1980s, giving us another 10 odd years of buffer, structural shifts might accelerate rapid erosion.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Technology, digitisation and artificial intelligence (AI) have already changed the nature of many jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These are skill sets that people born in the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s might not particularly equipped with or can be picked up easily.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our people also do not want to work at the same pace, cadence and intensity in their later years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How common is it to hear of friends saying that they wanted to slow it down?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But the treadmill seemingly can only go faster.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At the recent post-Budget dialogue with Tampines residents, a resident in his 50s commented with part joy and part exasperation that he might have to make a choice between caregiving for his grandchildren and his full-time work because there are rarely part-time work or slower work opportunities to go into.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has also fostered a re-thinking of work-life priorities and lead some older Singaporeans to exit the workforce permanently if unable to find a compromise.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We face a serious cliff-drop in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It can unsettle the economy and society fundamentally.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The questions before us are: are the older workers ready for the future jobs and are the jobs ready for the older workers?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, we need to make preparing for an ageing workforce an economy-wide priority.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It still rose on average between 2019 and 2022.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have also moved definitively to tackle ageism, a perennial complaint of older workers, through a proposed Workplace Fairness legislation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, these moves might not be sufficient for the future.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to include within each of the Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs) a pillar on creating and transforming "age-friendly" jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is no longer sufficient to create jobs that are of high economic value.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But we must also focus on jobs that our older Singaporeans can and will do.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The focus must rightly be so on bringing in jobs that grow the economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But in the entire value chain, we must identify jobs that mature workers can do well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I often wonder what is the percentage of available and upcoming jobs that would match the physical, mental and lifestyle needs of older Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to double down on our job redesign efforts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What is the number of jobs that will be redesigned over the years to match our ageing workforce?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This must be a number we track closely.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, I would like to share on the experience of SBS Transit (SBST).

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Older workers are a significant part of the company.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Maintenance, especially in the train systems, can be very laborious and physically taxing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We struggle to attract younger workers into the workforce like many other companies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To help the older workers aged above 55 years old to continue to be productive, SBST is redesigning jobs from the ground up.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They have an overhead catenary system or the electrical cables supplying power to the trains.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Inspection and maintenance require hard physical work with heavy equipment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Today, they use light-weight equipment such as laser-gauges.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Condition-based maintenance is practised to reduce physical deployment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Older workers are redeployed to inspection closer to ground than higher-level ones.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some workers had gone into mentorship or trainer roles.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: More than 50 maintenance crew have benefited from this change.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: More will benefit in the years to come.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Admittedly, it is a larger company with more resources.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need solutions for small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) which hire the bulk of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, we need to look at redesigning our work structure.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have often heard of mature workers hoping for part-time work or micro jobs but there is a dearth of them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But as it is a social compact imperative to pay more to support our lower-wage workers, perhaps it is also time for similar thinking for older workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can also consider private-public partnerships in fostering such part-time and micro jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In Japan, Silver Human Resources Centers have been established since 1975 as job agencies for seniors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These are membership-based organisations that provide older Japanese with temporary and short-term work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Public and municipal agencies leaned in to create and find work for older workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: An associated point is creating specialised centres that focus on helping our older workers to manage employment needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our current job placement ecosystem has worked well for the general needs of the workforce, but older workers have different needs such as a shorter training runway, physical limitations and life expectations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In 2017, Japan started the Hello Work Senior.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is a job placement agency specially catered for workers aged above 60 years old.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The service works with employers to understand their needs and preferences and match them with suitable older candidates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As geriatrics is a specialty within medicine, silver placement centres can have its special place in our placement ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our ageing workforce is also an opportunity to advance assistive technology to help workers work for longer and safer.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our public transport operators have already put in driver monitoring, collision avoidance and driver alertness technology.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many of our bus captains today are able to work well into their late-60s and beyond.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are many other industries, especially those with a significant number of older workers, that we must deep dive into.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must establish research centres dedicated to helping workers stay employed for longer.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Such research centres can focus on developing assistive technology, identifying jobs that may be more suited for senior workers and developing appropriate training to transit into such jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs), such as the Singapore Management University (SMU) Centre for Research on Successful Ageing, are a case in point.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Ministry consider looking into establishing such research centres?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Flexible work arrangement (FWA) is often cited as the solution to balance the needs of older workforce and business needs of companies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Indeed, it is an essential tool, not just for an older workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have made significant strides in expanding FWA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Tripartite guidelines are useful to guide tripartite progress in implementing FWA but we might need to take bolder steps in the near future.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We should rightly allow for voluntary take-up by companies because of the difficulties in implementation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can even grant monetary incentives to companies with progressive practices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But if progress does not meet our needs, we might need to consider giving workers certain rights to FWA to accelerate the scaling up of FWA efforts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Lastly, our ageing workforce also necessitates us to look into the roles played by our foreign workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As our people age, there is a significant need in certain industries such as healthcare and caregiving support, tradesman and craftsman work such as plumbing, air-condition servicing and carpentry.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Therefore, our foreign workforce framework will need to be more nuanced, differentiated and promote higher productivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There could be certain high-touch industries that we would want to keep for a larger core of older Singaporeans and there are other industries where we need more foreign support, especially those involving more physical work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The current broad-based sector-based approach would need to be more finely differentiated.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is difficult work and might require a multi-year effort.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The rapidly ageing population poses serious structural challenges to fiscal sustainability and economic growth.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: When older workers retire, they are also less able to deal with problems such as higher inflation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our younger workers are likely to shoulder heavier caregiving loads, with some even having to leave the workforce to do so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: If Singaporeans are unable to fill job openings, employers will have to look to foreign labour to do so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Only when both our jobs and our older workers are ready for each other, would we be able to manage this smouldering crisis.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, it is trite that SMEs form the backbone of our economy.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We encounter many SMEs in our day-to-day life, especially in retail, food and beverages (F&B) and commercial sectors.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: SMEs also form critical support for multinational corporations (MNCs).

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: My speech today will focus on the manpower challenges and obstacles faced by SME employers.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In my discussions with SME representatives, the issues of hiring and retaining staff have been raised repeatedly.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: SMEs have shared that they are not able to compete with large enterprises on equal footing.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Comparatively and in general, SMEs are not as well-resourced as large enterprises.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In some SMEs, their HR personnel are performing dual functions on top of their finance or administrative roles.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Consequently, the persons responsible for employment matters are not able to exclusively specialise and focus on their HR duties.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This exacerbates the problem since they may not succeed in hiring or may end up hiring staff who are unsuitable for their needs.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Having less resources also translates into being less able to put out attractive offers, the most important part of it would be remuneration.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There is also the issue of perceived branding and the prestige of the company in question.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Jobseekers may thus find larger enterprises more attractive and that their CVs will be bolstered for future prospects.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For small companies, the runway for progression and development may be limited such that prospective employees deem taking up such positions as heading towards a dead end even right from the beginning.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: How can we reasonably expect our SMEs to compete with larger enterprises and Government agencies for manpower from the same talent pool?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is made worse by the current inflationary pressures.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In my heart, I lamented the loss in management and specialised skills for the industries.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: However, I also understand when they said that the Grab job meant the convenience of having a car and the comfort of working in air-conditioning.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They are without the stresses of safety and the pressures of project delivery.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I thought about the loss of dependency ratio too if the companies cannot find local talent to take over such positions.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Chairman, many SMEs are and will remain increasingly hard-pressed to survive.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: SME employers' concerns stem from real issues that affect their companies and the livelihoods of all on the payroll, and the staff's families.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I implore the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) to address their concerns, real and perceived, to ensure that no SME is left behind in their journey towards growth and innovation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While employees rejoice as it gives us the flexibility to manage our daily lives, it also means that some jobs can be done remotely and hence can be done anywhere in the world.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, given our higher wages, how do we define the unique value proposition of our Singaporean workforce to the world?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we equip our workforce with competency and levels of productivity such that our Singaporean talents are relevant and add value to the global economy?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With remote working, how can our PMET workforce expand our horizon and gain access to jobs beyond our shores?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What skills must we equip the PMETs with and how do we develop these skills to ensure that our PMETs are competitive in the global talent market?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In April last year, I asked the Minister for Manpower whether the Ministry was looking into new strategies to improve the prospects of skilled trade jobs for Singaporeans such as licensed electricians and plumbers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It was a follow-up to my speech at the opening of Parliament this term.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The reply to the same Parliamentary Question I put to the Minister for Trade and Industry for licensed electrical workers (LEWs) was less granular.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The majority of the LEWs were between 41 and 80 years of age.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Unlike licensed plumbers, the number of Singaporeans who are LEWs was not directly revealed by the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI).

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such individuals earn middle-class wages and are an integral part of the economy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, he also stressed that the Labour Movement is not the Government and does not set national policy, including the scope of the PWM.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Apart from the strategic importance of having a strong Singaporean Core in skilled trade occupations, the simple fact is that these trades do not pay as well today and are less attractive than working in an office type or air-conditioned setting.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In view of the Minister's reply last April, can I inquire what efforts the Government intends to take to specifically target Singaporean workers into skilled trade jobs?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As a nation and society, it remains my view that a decisive shift to aggressively promote skilled trade jobs for Singaporeans would also alter our understanding of meritocracy, for the better.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is just a city and has no greater hinterland from which we could draw talent.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As such, we can rely only on our people as the primary fuel for our continued success.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Trending suggestions like a shorter work week or a right to disconnect – which, honestly, to me, Sir, as a lawyer, is an entirely foreign concept – are being echoed in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The gist of these trends is for employees to turn inwards, to prioritise personal comforts over career ambition.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These trends are also a particular phenomenon of advanced economies that enjoy some level of comfort.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Our Government has prudently started looking at these matters, ranging from mental health concerns to flexible working hours.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, we must be realistic that not all of our Singaporeans are or can become top global-level talent.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I am glad that MOM has introduced schemes in the past year to attract global talent to Singapore, which bolsters the resilience of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister elaborate on the future plans to continue to attract top talent to Singapore as well as how we will ensure that these talents are complementary with the Singapore workforce?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister also elaborate on how we can facilitate knowledge and skills transfer from foreign talents to Singaporeans so that we can level up Singaporeans in key areas that would be important in the future?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Mediating and settling such disputes early can help harmonious labour relations, which contributes to workforce resilience.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: With COVID-19 behind us, our businesses are looking forward to grow again.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How is the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) supporting businesses to address the lack of manpower availability issue?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: PWM and foreign labour policies do impact manpower costs.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How is MOM helping businesses to manage the costs increase?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore being open to global talent is not an option.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore needs a complementary foreign labour at all levels across most sectors.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How is MOM supporting businesses to attract local Singaporeans into their industry or sector, especially for job roles at or higher than the S Pass and Employment Pass qualifying salary levels?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How else is MOM doing to help businesses reduce reliance on foreign manpower?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: With a diverse workforce, it is imperative for good practices at the workplace.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And, finally, what is the Government doing to strengthen the alignment between jobs, skills and pay for value?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And how does the Public Service intend to model the way forward?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, in the age, sometimes called the Fourth Industrial Revolution, a critical question is how the arrival of robots enabled by artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning affects the pay and employment of workers.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: A stark case economists study is where a robot is a perfect substitute for a human worker, able to do exactly what the human worker is able to do.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In this case, it is clear that the arrival of robots is like an influx of identical workers into the economy, with its given technology and stock of machines and land.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Such technology which might be called automation technology has the feature that acts to replace humans in a range of tasks and does not boost labour productivity.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: This is, however, not likely to be the complete story, especially over the medium to long term.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: There are other channels that might deliver more positive results on wage growth and as a consequence of adopting robots.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The question to be asked is how can we harness the opportunities and face head on the threats of AI in order to benefit our workers.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: For example, with deep learning algorithms developed by scientists within the AI community machines are enabled to learn, to a certain extent, without human supervision.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Workers doing medical research are able to take advantage of deep learning to sieve through and analyse large amounts of medical data.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: This might boost the productivity of workers and further raise their wage earnings.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: What can be done to encourage the development and application of robots that perform tasks which are complementary to workers who are employed in the retail and food and beverage (F&B) sectors?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Second, the arrival of robots sometimes stimulates investment in conventional machines, equipment and physical structures, which will then exert an upward pull on wage rates.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: This channel might confer benefits to both high-wage and lower-wage workers.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In conventional growth theory, the law of diminishing returns operates so that in the absence of steady technical progress, capital accumulation gradually slows down as each additional unit of capital fetches a lower rate of return.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: This acts to pull up the wages of workers across the whole distribution of skills.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In what specific industries might capital investment be stimulated as a result of the adoption of robots?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Third, the arrival of robots by causing some workers in the economy to shift from participating in production to participating in innovative activity, might ultimately shift up the whole wage path because it stimulates innovation and thus the overall productivity of workers.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: There can be further research in the area of AI that can restructure the production process adopted in Singapore to create new high productivity tasks that can be performed by human workers.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: AI-enabled individualised teaching methods might raise the demand for educators who have the skills to apply these methods to meet the diverse needs of students.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Augmented reality technology might also enable workers to work alongside machines to execute high-precision tasks in advanced manufacturing.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: How can we identify potential applications of AI to our local landscape to boost worker productivity?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, the arrival of robots produces threats when they simply replace human workers in a set of tasks and thus depresses workers wage earnings.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: However, the arrival of robots can also provide opportunities for workers if AI can be harnessed to create new complementary tasks that raise labour productivity.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It is likely that a society-wide approach is needed to maximise the opportunities of AI and to mitigate the threats to the workforce.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Although we want companies to invest in job redesigns and technologies to improve their productivity, such transformation will take much time and resources to plan and realise.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: To transform, companies require specific new areas of expertise that are short of relevant local talents, for example, in the areas of sustainability and digital.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: In the built environment sector, it has also lost many highly skilled hands-on or craft-based labour.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: They are critical even as we try to transform the sector towards higher productivity.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: In view of the unprecedented confluence of challenges companies are facing, how can the Government better help companies to deal with the immediate labour shortages, while supporting their transformation?

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Government adopt a variegated approach to allow more foreign workers to supplement local workers for such roles?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, I would like to make a call for all employers to make and ensure our Singaporeans become the Core of the total workforce.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Our education system is considered one of the best in the world and we must be worried if this does not lead to job opportunities for them.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Aside from our high standards of education system, we also have many adult training centres that should be able to equip our resident workforce with the required necessary skillsets.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: When NTUC launched Worker 4.0, it was aimed at transforming our resident workforce by going through trainings in three broad areas: Adaptability, Technological and Technical.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The use of technology has started even before COVID-19 struck the world.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: With COVID-19, it only accelerated the use of technology at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We should not make technology replace our workers but rather encourage our workers to embrace technology during their course of work for better outcomes.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Employers should identify training providers that can provide technological knowledge for their workforce at both their and their workers' convenience.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Do engage NTUC Learning Hub, whose theme is to "learn anytime and anywhere".

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: To all my fellow workers, let us continue to learn, unlearn and relearn skills so that your management finds it difficult and more challenging to release you.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: For employers, always look around internally and ask if you have done justice to our resident workforce with your ratio of locals to foreigners.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: During our NTUC-Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF) PME Taskforce consultations, surveys and focus groups as well as in our latest #EveryWorkerMatters conversations, mature PMEs, especially those above 40 years of age, are anxious about the prospects of their employment and employability.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In this respect, I have three suggestions for MOM.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, I refer to the recently released interim report of the Tripartite Committee on Workplace Fairness.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Progress Singapore Party (PSP) has high hopes of the Committee which was set up just before debate on foreign talent policy in September 2021.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we have found the interim report to be inadequate in at least two areas.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We hope the Committee will consider and incorporate our views in the final report.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, there is an inadequate focus on the job security of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As it is quite unlikely that foreigners will complain about discrimination when they have no automatic right to work in Singapore, many of these complaints must be from Singaporeans complaining that the foreigners have been preferred.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope the new legislation would enforce meaningful changes in the quality, number and concentration of foreign work pass holders that the Government, including the Prime Minister, have identified as potential problems in July 2021.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Stronger actions can be taken to ensure that our workplaces remain diverse.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will be a stronger safeguard than COMPASS in ensuring their workplaces do not become communal enclaves where one foreign nationality is favoured over others.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To complement that policy, we should also take out Recommendation 9, which provides exemptions for SMEs that employ less than 25 employees.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a potential loophole that will allow larger companies to set up subsidiaries that employ one local and 24 foreign PMETs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is urgently needed to level the playing field for Singaporean PMEs because employers will have to pay more and more CPF contributions for Singaporeans as the ordinary wage ceiling is raised, making Singaporeans less competitive on wages compared to foreigners.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second area that I am concerned about is the secular nature of our workplace and employment laws.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This appears to be a reversal of MOM's stance in 2013.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At that time, a pregnant church employee was sacked in the seventh month of her pregnancy because she had conceived a child in an extramarital relationship against church teachings.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MOM intervened to secure compensation for her because employment law had been violated.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MOM also stressed that workplaces must be preserved as a secular space in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thus, I hope the Minister can clarify how Recommendation 10 is aligned with MOM's stance in 2013 or whether MOM's stance has changed since then.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is in line with the spirit of repealing section 377A and will better protect LGBT workers from discrimination based on their sexuality, which still exists in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: LGBT workers should be allowed to earn a living on a level playing field based on merit, like anyone else in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is the employment rate of unvaccinated citizens back on par with vaccinated citizens for each age group?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, workplace fairness is an important issue.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The PSP is glad that the Government will be enshrining this in law next year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But when drafting the law, I hope the Government will enforce a level playing field for Singaporeans and ensure that workplaces remain secular.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Discrimination faced by PwDs can range from exploitation and denigration to stereotyping and displaying patronising attitudes towards them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is important to ensure that this legislation provides sufficient protection for PwDs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To achieve this, the law should incorporate several key provisions, which have also been recommended by the Disabled People's Association.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A reasonable accommodation is a modification to a job or work environment that enables a qualified PwD to perform the essential functions of the job and have the same employment opportunities as their abled colleagues without imposing an unreasonable burden on the employer.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore has ratified the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) a decade ago.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Article 27 of the CRPD requires signatories to take appropriate steps, including legislation, to ensure that reasonable accommodation is provided to PwDs in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Examples of reasonable accommodations may include providing screen readers, installing ramps, offering FWAs or conducting meetings online.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Enshrining these provisions in the anti-discrimination legislation will ensure that it is effective in preventing PwDs from being excluded from the workforce.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We need to change societal attitudes to foster inclusivity in the workplace for PwDs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Rather than viewing PwDs as beneficiaries of charity, we must recognise them as individuals and workers who possess equal rights and contribute valuable skills to the workforce.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Is the Ministry looking to do more to highlight the contributions of PwDs in the workplace?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The recommendations in the interim report by the Tripartite Committee on Workplace Fairness is one that is greatly anticipated.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The inclusion of characteristics such as sex, marital status, pregnancy status and caregiving responsibilities are of particular significance to the NTUC's Woman and Family Unit.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Labour Movement has for decades worked to ensure women in the workplace are given a positive and safe work environment to achieve their career aspirations.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The enshrining of such protections will help in our fight towards eliminating workplace discrimination faced by women.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Yet, the NTUC Women's Committee has noted that women continue to face workplace discrimination.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For many of the women who feel such discrimination, they often find it difficult to articulate their grievances clearly or they lack the right channels or opportunities to do so.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Employers, too, especially SMEs, have often told us that they lack the resources and know-how to address such situations.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we welcome the legislation to come, we know we have miles to go before we sleep and welcome it.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Maybe in practice, it may prove to be a daunting task.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We call on the Ministry to work with the Labour Movement in empowering and equipping our workers to be able to provide clear articulation of discrimination grievances and seek clarification on how the Ministry will engage and support companies in effectively implementing workplace fairness practices.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Chairman, I declare my interest as a member of the Tripartite Committee on Workplace Fairness.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I am glad that MOM has accepted the recommendations of the NTUC-SNEF PME Taskforce and we are going to introduce a dedicated workplace fairness piece of legislation as well as a points system via COMPASS to regulate the issuance of Employment Passes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: On the same note, can MOM also update us on the Fair Consideration Framework and the number and type of cases reported, investigated and closed at Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP) thus far?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I will also wish to ask the status of the Strengthening the Singaporean Core efforts and suggest if we can publish the triple weak list of companies as the workplace fairness piece of legislation will only be introduced in the latter half of 2024 and is effective 2025 and beyond.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Also, after the new piece of legislation, what will be the status of the Fair Consideration Framework, TAFEP as well as the watchlist?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, we currently have a tight labour market.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our low total fertility rate (TFR) means we need a foreign workforce to complement our local workforce to compete globally.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Other countries are waging a war for global talent.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Countries such as New Zealand and Hong Kong already have measures to attract foreign talent post-COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must bring in foreign workforce with the right skills and qualifications and at the right price.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is always a delicate balance between meeting our labour needs and protecting our citizens' interests.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One concern is that the influx of foreign workforce may exacerbate the shortage of housing in Singapore, causing rental prices to go up.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does the Government plan to balance housing required for these foreigners and the need for affordable properties to rent for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In the same token, foreigners may be deterred from working in Singapore due to high rents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What are the Government's plans to assuage these concerns?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister also share updates to our foreign workforce policies, including COMPASS?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What can we expect from the upcoming workplace fairness legislation that is to be enacted?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What is MOM doing to promote technology and productivity-enhancing measures in our workplaces?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What else can we do to incentivise companies to invest in automation and other technologies?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we equip workers with the skills needed to thrive in a tech-enabled workplace?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: The Shortage Occupation List (SOL) is one of the criteria in the COMPASS framework.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: MOM has said that the first SOL will be announced this month.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: It is expected to identify occupations requiring skills that are currently in shortage in the local workforce.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Could the Minister share what occupations will be included in the SOL?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Will the SOL take into account the pipeline of local ITE, polytechnic and university graduates in both local and foreign institutions?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: For example, if there are many local graduates in, say, information and communications technology (ICT) next year, the SOL should be revised accordingly.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: With the knowledge of skill shortages in the SOL, schools, tertiary institutions and adult education centres can better plan their curriculum and intake size to better prepare local students and workers to fill them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: The Government should work closely with ITEs, polytechnics and universities to expand their intake of courses for occupations in the SOL.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I hope it will be reviewed frequently so that it can be responsive to changes in industry requirements and we will not have situations where an occupation remains on the SOL when there is sufficient local talent in that area.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: This could prompt firms to search harder for available local talent before turning to foreigners.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: All these can create more opportunities for Singaporeans in the workplace and reduce the heavy reliance on foreigners in our workforce.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The problem seems to have worsened as we resumed most of our economic activities post-COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many businesses lamented that there may well be more businesses to do or more growth opportunities out there but there are not really enough workers to go around to grab these opportunities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many ask for a higher foreign worker quota and/or for MOM to loosen the foreign worker criteria.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In fact, we are leveraging and dependent on a large pool of foreign labour to stretch our overall economic capacity and growth potential.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There are physical and social limits as to how much more foreign labour we can accommodate on our tiny island.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I believe we are already near the limits in terms of numbers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Being too dependent on foreign manpower also expose us to source country risks as well as concentration risks.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have seen these vulnerabilities played out during the pandemic when borders were closed or restricted.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask the Minister for an update as to how the businesses have coped with the foreign manpower constraints?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Have we seen noticeable shifts in companies tapping on technologies and training to improve productivity and capabilities?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The COMPASS framework was introduced as a transparent system to strengthen the complementarity and diversity of our workforce and prevent sources concentration.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These are targeted schemes that comes with tight conditions to fulfil and also with a specific percentage and number cap to limit the number of foreign workers a firm can hire.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the case of M-SEP, participating companies must also commit to hiring and training local workers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In this regard, may I ask the Minister if there are any updates to our foreign workforce policies to attain these goals?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Rising prices threaten our retired seniors' ability to meet growing expenses, where they do not enjoy the benefit of rising wages now.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have raised a few questions on retirement adequacy in my Budget debate speech.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is it time to adjust the allocation ratios such that a greater percentage is allocated into the Special Account instead of the Ordinary and Medisave Accounts?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on Singaporeans' retirement adequacy?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How do we assist retiree households that have limited ability to accommodate expenditure shocks, outlived their savings or never accumulated much to begin with?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad
text: Chairman, the topic of retirement adequacy has been attracting attention and interest among our fellow workers, from the young to the golden generation.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad
text: I appreciate the Government stepping up their efforts to ensure that our workers have enough for their basic retirement sum when they reach 55 years old.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad
text: This will certainly help our workers CPF savings and make this as part of their corporate social responsibility (CSR).

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad
text: How many actually take up the Enhanced Retirement Sum when they reach 55?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad
text: How many Singaporeans have actually put their property as a provision to match the difference between the Basic and Full Enhanced Retirement Sums so that they can cash out at the age of 55?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad
text: For every Singaporean, we dream to retire with enough wealth for our retirement years with income and good health as a serious matter.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad
text: Once again, I strongly believe our fellow Singaporeans look forward to such support of not to reduce CPF contributions at the age of 55 for those that are doing well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Chairman, on the topic of enhancing CPF returns, I would like to once again take the chance to raise concerns that I have previously voiced out in Parliament in the past two years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The CPF scheme plays an important role in securing Singaporeans' retirement needs and it is after all the CPF Board's mission.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: An opportunity to enhance these returns is therefore something which many Singaporeans continuously look out for.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The long lines at the banks recently due to the promotional fixed deposit rates is evidence enough of this demand.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the past month alone, major banks such as OCBC and DBS have begun offering additional products for investors to allocate their CPF Ordinary Account (OA) monies to.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Again, the long lines forming suggest that Singaporeans' needs for higher quality returns to their OA funds is largely unmet.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The excess demand for these additional OA investment products despite their rather modest long-term returns as compared to a globally diversified portfolio of Exchange-traded Funds (ETFs) for example, further shows that there is pent-up demand for more investment options that need to be satiated.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In Budgets 2021 and 2022, I sought clarification on the CPF Lifetime Retirement Investment Scheme (LRIS).

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Last year, I asked if the Expert Investment Council had completed their studies and if the Government was still considering rolling out the LRIS.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Is there a more concrete timetable on which the Ministry can share details of the proposed LRIS?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I hope the Ministry is cognisant that the longer the delay, the higher the opportunity cost and real cost to Singaporeans' retirement savings.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, I would like to reiterate the lack of options currently available to Singaporeans to allow them to take better control of the wealth they have.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Since my speech last year, there are still only six ETFs available for Singaporeans to invest in.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With increasing financial literacy among our people, they should be empowered to take greater charge of their investment decisions according to their risk appetites and financial goals.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The CPF Board's vision is, among others, to enable Singaporeans to have a secure retirement through lifelong income.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is imperative that we therefore consistently review and revise, where necessary, the mechanisms that underlie its functions to ensure that it serves its purpose as effectively as possible.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: One of the key concerns frustrating Singaporeans now is inflation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I understand that the liquidity of Ordinary Accounts (OA) pegs them to shorter-term interest rates.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, for much of our working lives, the bulk of our CPF contributions gets allocated towards the OA.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I appreciate the interest rate floor that has been put in place at 2.5%.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, we must balance CPF OA rates against the goal of preserving the purchasing power of our retirement funds and guarding against inflation over time.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Pegging OA interest rates to deposit rates has its issues as it can be quite arbitrary.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For example, DBS states that the 12-month fixed deposit rates for deposits up to $19,999 is 3.2%, while an amount of $20,000, which is used for OA calculations, drops to 0.05% instead.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We are beginning to see a stark contrast in rates.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Recent news articles show banks competing with one another to get deposits.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: UOB has even raised its maximum bonus rates from 3.6% to 7.8%, while many now offer fixed deposit rates at 3% to 4%.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Chairman, the OA formula itself has remained unchanged since 1999.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Many of us now have the likes of a DBS Multiplier or UOB ONE account where higher interest rates can be earned easily as compared to historical savings accounts.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even if the Government does not wish to take inflation into account, I urge the Government to reconsider the formula after 24 years, to take into account the current nature of fixed deposits and savings rates from the three local banks so that it better reflects economic realities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The fact of the extension itself indicates that the previous HSP did not adequately meet its objectives.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: For the built environment sector, in particular, do major safety lapses occur in the context of subcontracting work where margins for profits and time to complete work may be narrower and are safety lapses more prevalent here?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I understand that effort is being put into this issue of workplace fatalities and major injuries, but may I ask what the Government is going to do differently when implementing these new 2023 recommendations?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Does the Ministry foresee a deeper cultural shake-up required in the attitudes towards workplace safety?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: How are fatalities and major injuries going to be arrested in a more significant way?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mr Chairman, in my Budget debate speech, I expressed my dismay at the current poor workplace safety outcomes, which resulted in the tragic loss of lives, many of which were due to basic errors that could have and should have been avoided.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The spike in workplace fatalities in the past few months might have been a sign that companies are relaxing their stringent Workplace Safety and Health (WSH) practices as the Heightened Safety Period (HSP) draws nearer to its end.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must build a culture where workers feel safe to report unsafe work practices that they see at their worksites.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must entrench a culture where employers must realise that unsafe practices cannot go unreported and cannot be swept under the carpet.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Can MOM provide an update on the WSH feedback rate, across its various channels, over the past five years?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Can MOM review and enhance its feedback structures, and where needed, to create new reporting channels that make it easier for anyone, including a member of public, to report unsafe work practices?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As such, I urge MOM to focus efforts on the high-risk sectors which account disproportionately for the number of workplace injuries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I urge the Ministry to enhance outreach and funding support for SMEs to adopt and deploy WSH technologies.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I have previously highlighted how such technologies have improved safety standards at the workplace, especially in high-risk environments.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Labour Movement stands ready to work closely with our tripartite partners to do all we can to help every worker return home safely at the end of every workday.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, there has been recent debate over the provision of chairs at retail outlets and the right of retail workers to sit.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Multiple studies report there are significant health risks associated with prolonged standing, including chronic venous insufficiency, musculoskeletal disorders as well as spontaneous abortion for pregnant women in some rare cases.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is a health hazard caused by an inability to alternate muscle usage.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Countries like Malaysia and South Africa have enacted laws on the right to sit.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The UK requires retail outlets to provide seats and to allow staff to sit occasionally.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Our laws and regulations should promote our retail workers' health, well-being and longevity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, we need to better recognise and value skill sets in the job market.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While there are continuing efforts to address starting salaries and career progression for different job roles and sectors, more can be done to address the growing wage disparity between graduates and non-graduates.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As our workforce becomes increasingly competitive, a widening gap can lead to negative outcomes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We do not wish for a situation where many young and promising Singaporeans would eventually feel undervalued despite having the relevant skill sets simply because of a lack of necessary qualifications.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mitigating such outcomes does not mean to devalue paper qualifications but it is about having an equal recognition for skills and competencies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the US, companies like Google and IBM have reportedly reduced the need for paper qualifications in some tech roles.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: IBM has shifted away from degree requirements with less than one-third of its IT jobs requiring one.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We do not see Google and IBM being less competitive in the tech world when changing its focus on one’s level of competency.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is a greater need to recognise skills especially craftmanship.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am supportive of this model which has a clear framework and structured skills training so that quality standards can be assured.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This can provide a further guide to fairly align salary range with levels of skills.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While we push for nationwide efforts to recognise and value skills the same way as one’s qualifications, such a change will require human resource (HR) managers and employers to take the first step.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: HR managers are key to making structural changes and fine-tuning workplace policies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Since COVID-19, the role of a HR manager has significantly evolved which includes the need for more nuanced recruitment as an increasingly complex economy requires more differentiated skills.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With constant changes to our economy, HR managers also have to be involved in redesigning jobs for the employees.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While HR managers obtain the relevant expertise in their expanded role, they would also need to refresh their knowledge on job roles and the necessary skill sets.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, I would like to ask how MOM would assist employers and HR managers to better understand the granularity of each profession and skills requirement which dovetails with SSG’s skills framework so that recruitment is not merely based on paper qualifications but also on skills certifications.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Overall, we must also not neglect our SMEs, especially micro ones which do not have the necessary resources to expand HR roles.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To help our SMEs cope with the evolving needs of aHR manager, I would re-emphasise on the need for a chief human resources officer (CHRO) as a similar service to the Infocomm Media Development Authority’s (IMDA)’s Chief Technology Officer-as-a-service.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such a service can support SMEs in access to gain access to HR resources and expertise.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Good human resource (HR) practices and processes are an essential ingredient if we wish to foster a fair and inclusive workplace.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: One way this can be achieved is by having certified HR professionals in our organisations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I have three suggestions to the Ministry of Manpower (MOM).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Second, is for the IHRP certification course and examinations to include the knowledge of the concept of tripartism including all the requisite tripartite standards, guidelines and advisories as well as working with unions and the industrial relations system.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Third, HR cannot be the sole custodians of progressive practices.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: People Managers also play a critical role in supporting and cascading good human capital practices in the organisation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I believe more can be done in this respect and professional bodies like the IHRP can work with partners like Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF) and NTUC Learning Hub, Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) and HR associations to equip People Managers with the requisite skills and knowledge to better engage and nurture their workforce.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The Ministry of Manpower (MOM) together with tripartite partners also conduct regular public education and outreach efforts to raise awareness of the PWM and its requirements among employers and workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: However, as with any policy or regulation, there may be instances where employers are not fully compliant with the PWM requirements, be it in the terms of technical requirements or in spirit.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In this regard, I would like to ask MOM to give an update on this implementation and what measures are in place or explore enforcement strategies or mechanisms to ensure that companies comply to PWM wages and other requirements.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: The Labour Movement's Progressive Wage Model (PWM) is key to protecting our vulnerable as it uplifts our lower-wage workers' livelihoods while equipping our workers the requisite training to upscale and improve.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: The PWM was also introduced into occupations – administration and driving – recently.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: As the chairperson for the tripartite clusters for retail and food services, I note the significance of these clusters to be included in the PWM framework.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: These are very relatable industries for many Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: The workers in these industries touch the hearts and lives of Singaporeans daily and the businesses' innovations and achievements put Singapore in the world map as a true global city.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Given that we hope to attract more talented young Singaporeans into these industries, can the Ministry provide an update on how it will support and encourage companies to embrace attractive career ladders and drum up productivity?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: I note too that these industries were the first predominantly business-to-consumer (B2C) industries to introduce the PWM framework.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: As such, supporting our lower-wage workers would include consumers as a stakeholder.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: We call on the Ministry to work with the Labour Movement to bring home the message that uplifting the lives of our lower-wage Singaporeans is a whole of community effort.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Migrant workers are more vulnerable to unsafe workplace practices because of their limited bargaining power.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: They need employers’ consent to transfer to a new job, save exceptions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: If they provide evidence of unsafe work, they should be allowed to resign without notice and stay here for two months to find another employer if that evidence is borne out.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Second, they should be allowed to transfer if they have been working for at least one year with their current employer with a one-month notice period without their current employer being allowed to cancel their Work Permit during that period.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: This will incentivise employers to create safer, decent work environments.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Also, can MOM empower workers to call out unsafe work practices?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: When settling in, MOM can assure them that whistle-blowers’ identities are kept confidential and they will be protected from dismissal.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: MOM can reward whistle-blowers if complaints are found to be valid.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: An issue is that the WICA insurers become “gatekeepers” who determine which claims are valid before compensation is assessed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: This creates a conflict of interest since insurers might be incentivised to deny validity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: In 2019, the then-Minister of State said MOM was rolling out a system of checks and balances.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Has MOM reviewed the performance of WICA insurers to see if this system is adequate?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Does MOM proactively monitor each insurer’s performance or does it only investigate complaints?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: How does MOM ensure that designated insurers comply with stipulated timelines for processing claims?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The WICA insurers’ manual should be published so the public can hold insurers accountable and report potential non-compliance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Can MOM also review the use of an independent assessor such as the Commissioner of Labour previously?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: This is done in New Zealand and Ireland.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Many migrant workers prefer to cook their own food; secondly, can the Singapore Food Agency (SFA) consider mandating that catered food is delivered in safe eating conditions as per the National Environment Agency (NEA) regulations applicable for cooked food supplied by caterers for events?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: If this means food storage or a shift towards freezers and microwaves, so be it.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, those earning above $2,500 will also have difficulties adjusting to a lower take-home pay.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If this is the case, then those who opt in will cost the platform owners more than those who opt out.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is desirable for more platform workers to opt in so that they have more retirement savings.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, my concern is whether those who opt in would be discriminated against because they are more costly.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, is the decision to either opt in or out of CPF a one-off decision?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, the freelancer community of coaches and instructors in the fields of sports, fitness, learning, and visual and performing arts are an important part of Singapore’s economy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As an adviser to the NTUC affiliate, the National Instructors and Coaches Association, I seek MOM’s attention to uplift this group of freelancers for their better job and income security and well-being.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Much has been done for platform workers and lower-wage workers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The freelancer community too should be paid fairly, based on their skills, contributions and track records.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Today, many of them are often the price takers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They are hesitant in adjusting their contract rates even when there are valid reasons to do so such as rising business costs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: When contracts are up, there is often the fear of losing contracts to the lowest bidder should they charge higher.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They face constraints even with clients such as those in public agencies like the Ministry of Education (MOE), People’s Association (PA) or Health Promotion Board (HPB) as the client staff may find it hard to seek approvals for rate hikes mid-contract because of already approved fixed budgets and the need for additional paperwork to get approvals for adjustments.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I urge MOM to facilitate the development of a procurement guide to ensure a sustainable win-win arrangement and fair compensation for the freelancer community starting with their public sector clients.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many freelance instructors and coaches face limited access to resources such as class facilities, equipment or training materials.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Uplifting them can include providing them with greater access to sports or school facilities or through Government grants.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Freelancers too need lifelong learning and support to ensure they remain relevant and competitive.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, curate and provide local and overseas professional development opportunities to help them stay updated with the latest developments in their industries.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: The influence of platform workers is clear for us to see.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: They have become an integral part of our daily urban lives having transformed the way we eat, shop and move.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: While we celebrate the benefits and rewards such work brings, we cannot overlook the potential risks that an increasing number of platform workers face, be it the rising concerns over adequate retirement savings, health safety nets and housing.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: To this end, the Labour Movement is encouraged that the Government recognised these concerns.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: We thank the Government for accepting the 12 recommendations provided by the advisory committee on platform workers that will strengthen our social and livelihood safety nets for our platform workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: While the advisory committee looks towards the working group to deliberate on the details of the operationalisation of these recommendations, our platform workers have voiced their concerns on how the introduction of CPF may affect their take-home earnings and subsequently their livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: We hence welcomed the move to introduce a CPF transition support which will help alleviate these concerns.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Further, we call on the Ministry to work closely with the Labour Movement and our platform associations to ensure that there is fair apportionment of CPF contributions between the platform worker and the platform company.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: For many platform workers, a day of work is also a day of painful loss revenues.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: In addition to the insurance benefits for work injuries as put forth in the recommendations, we call for the Ministry to consider further safety nets for platform workers who are injured in the course of their work, through added healthcare subsidies and enhanced injuries and loss of income plans.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: As we look to strengthen our social compact, we must not forget to turn our attention to our vulnerable Singaporeans who are on the fringes and support them in their desire to earn decent livelihoods and the opportunity to contribute back to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Chairman, we need to push for improvement in senior employability and encourage those who wish to work to continue.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Second, to truly understand whether Singaporeans have sufficient retirement adequacy, we need to move beyond subsistence level retirement and develop a formal definition of what defines a decent quality of life in old age.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: In 2019, a team of local researchers derived the amount of money needed for seniors to achieve a basic standard of living in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Does the Ministry stand by its results or does MOM plan to do its own in-depth study?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Moreover, with high inflation in the past two years, is it time to review this amount?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Third, we can do more on the labour front by having more flexible work options.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Many older workers would like to work part-time and even go back and forth between periods of work and leisure.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Some want to spend more time with their families.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Others wish to travel and take care of their grandchildren and return to work after.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: There are a few ways companies can implement this and older workers can be allowed to take a few months' leave and then return to the job.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Coverage of duties would have to be arranged with flexibility and creativity exercise.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: We also should push on with job sharing and micro jobs which have been raised several times before.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: We should also consider the concept of phased retirement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: This allows seniors to gradually decrease the number of workdays a week until retirement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: We must continue to make progress towards improving retirement adequacy and senior employability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: For the seniors who derive employment from their work, we can help maintain their physical and mental well-being whilst also providing financial security.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: Chairman, retirement adequacy remains an important concern for many senior citizens in Singapore, especially in an inflationary environment because it can erode purchasing power of retirement savings over time.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: As the costs of living increases, the value of retirement savings may decrease, making it more difficult for seniors to meet their basic needs and maintain the standard of living in retirement.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: Additionally, healthcare cost tends to increase with age which can put further pressure on retirement savings.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: These factors can create financial insecurity and make it difficult for seniors to meet their retirement goals.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: As a result, it is important for the Government and individuals to take steps to address retirement adequacy in an inflationary environment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Deputy Prime Minister highlighted how we want to help our seniors age with grace, dignity and security.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Having good healthcare and retirement funds are important.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But none of these are a substitute for time with their children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Just last Saturday, a resident shared during my home visit at Block 205 that he needed leave from work to bring his mother for her repeated medical appointments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Legislating parent care leave will let Singaporeans be there to care for their parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure the Government feels the same way.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: When DORSCON Green was announced, many Singaporeans shared their fears of having to go back to the pre-COVID-19 way of work – and this has for the most part been quite true.
