speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: In fact, many bosses are asking their staff to work from the office, with a preference to "see" their staff working, for fear of them not producing work.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: As I shared in my Budget debate speech, one friend quipped that his boss said, and I paraphrase, "if you are not in the office, how do I know that you are working?" This old myth needs debunking.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I have mentioned in my previous speeches how other governments have legislated and are looking at ways to strengthen worker’s rights to FWAs, with the key intent on creating a more inclusive work environment for all.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Given the numerous benefits FWA has on women, young parents and the overall well-being of an individual, this should not be seen as a “good to have” or “extra”, but as part and parcel of what companies should offer to their employees.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: We had an opportunity to experience what it could look like to have FWAs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I hope that my worst fears of a return to pre-COVID-19 workplace norms in Singapore will not come true.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Even as many of us at work transit to the new normal, one thing we hope remains the same, Flexible Work Arrangements (FWAs).

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: In creating safe and inclusive workplaces, one must not only eliminate discrimination regarding the "who" at work, but also the "how" we choose to engage in our work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: FWAs have proven to be key to allowing employees achieve better work-life harmony and it can promote a more engaged and productive workforce, allowing our workers to accomplish their tasks at work while meeting their personal responsibilities at home.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: The recommendations of the Tripartite Committee on Workplace Fairness go hand-in-hand with FWAs, providing the flexibility to accommodate back-to-work women who have to take care of young children or elderly loved ones is a function of ensuring that women who hold multiple roles both at work and at home are not discriminated against for the outsized role we women play in society.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: FWAs also not limited merely to that of location but can also be extended to work hours, the work week and even work tasks.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Given the difficulties many industries face regarding manpower, employers need to be ingenious and creative in its adoption of FWAs to ensure that we can maximise our workforce and this can start with our back-to-work women who possess both the skills and desire to return to work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Recognising the importance of FWAs, I seek the Ministry's clarifications on how it attempts to encourage more companies to continue to embrace FWAs and, in particular, performance appraisals, job and culture redesign, to support women with caregiving responsibilities to say in their jobs or to return to the workplace seamlessly after a hiatus in their careers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: For example, call centre operators or help desk providers can be done remotely via FWAs and this can create opportunities for seniors, PwDs and part-time workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Another possibility is to fund training for seniors to be trained as trainers to impart their knowledge to the industry.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Given our ageing population and more of our seniors wanting to find employment although at a slower pace, how do we create structural employment opportunities for seniors through job redesign?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Similarly, how can we create structural employment opportunities for PwDs?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: In Pasir Ris, we have a few families with adult children with either mild autism or low IQ.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: One such family in my constituency has three children with disabilities in their 20s and 30s.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: The father is the sole breadwinner and the parents are worried for the future of the children.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: The children have not been able to find employment and are stuck at home all day.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Is there an opportunity for us to encourage businesses to also employ PwDs?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: How do we ensure that these fundings translate to actual improvements in employment opportunities for seniors, PwDs and part-time workers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: I am heartened to see that while we work towards growing our economy and equipping our workers with the right skill sets, we are also focusing on strengthening our social compact by ensuring growth is inclusive and we have work-life balance for workers in mind.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Anecdotally, through interactions with residents in Pasir Ris, it seems that post-pandemic, a small percentage of workers are either working entirely from home or are going back to work every weekday and the larger proportion of our PMET workforce are on a three plus two or two plus three arrangements of working remotely and working from office.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Has the number of complaints of perceived unfairness brought about by FWAs increase?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: However, not much information was provided on what the respondents meant by their being “too disabled” to work.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It would be important for us to find out whether there is a group of PwDs from within the 77% who are actually work-capable but have stayed out of the workforce because they are not aware of what to do or do not believe that there are jobs or workplaces that can accommodate their disability.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In better understanding their job search experiences, we can then identify their barriers to participating in the workforce and thus work towards reducing these barriers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In conjunction with the vision for Singapore as an inclusive society in 2030, I would like to ask the Minister for Manpower if they have further insights gathered from the survey on work-capable PwDs outside the workforce, and how Singapore can raise the workforce participation rate of working-age PwDs?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As mentioned in my Budget speech, caregivers of people with severe disabilities find great challenges in the work options that allow them to fulfil their ongoing caregiving responsibilities while financially supporting the high medical expenses and future retirement needs for themselves and their wards.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Flexibility regarding work hours and work spaces as well as the ability to take leave when required, are essential for these caregivers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This is because their wards are not work-capable and require consistent care, and caregivers need to be responsive to sudden or emergency needs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Those who are offered jobs tend to be for roles that underemployed them with significantly lower pay, a trade off that caregivers accept for the flexibility accorded.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Yet, even with these lowered job expectations, such Flexible Work Arrangements (FWAs) are not easily accessible, as caregivers often are confronted with interviewers and work cultures that have biases against working caregivers of FWAs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: One country that has explored support initiatives for working caregivers is the UK.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In the recent years, the UK has seen an uptrend in the number of working caregivers, whether supporting seniors or children.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In 2022, this number was one in five residents.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: To support them, the UK Civil Service launched an initiative called the Carer's Passport.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This Passport provides caregivers and their employers with information about how employees' caring responsibilities impact their work and provides a guided conversation on the flexibility needed to combine work and care.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It aims to balance the needs of the employee with the needs of the business.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Since its launch in 2010, the Carer's Passport has rolled out to hospitals, employers, communities, schools and universities across the UK.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I am hopeful that Singapore will one day see value in moving towards such an initiative, given our aging population and also push for larger families and hence, an increasing need for caregivers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: After all, close to three-quarter of our caregivers in Singapore are employed.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: How may we continue to encourage companies to make FWAs available for a larger range of job competencies, so that our caregivers can support themselves more sustainably?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: After many years of caregiving, caregivers of Persons with Disabilities (PwDs) who have found alternative caregiving options, find it hard to re-enter the workplace due to concerns over age and experience.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In their job search, they struggle with the lack of recognition of caregiving skills on the job market, despite their transferability.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These skills can range from project and time management, expanded skills in empathy and stress tolerance, as well as communication skills as they navigate conflict situations in caregiving.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Support to identify and recognise these skills in the workplace would be of great value to caregivers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In interviews, they are uncertain whether how much to share about their caregiving responsibilities for fear of discrimination or negative repercussions on their career due to possible biases by employers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Studies have shown that people with disabilities (PwDs) are poorer and more financially insecure than non-disabled people.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Granted that some may have the benefit of parents who are able to set up a trust for them via the Special Needs Trust company, not all PwDs have similar access.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: For non-work-capable PwDs, their caregivers become the main source of financial security.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These caregivers spend a large portion of their finances for the treatment of their severely disabled child and ward.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: With that, we may see that those who spend most of their lives caring for their loved ones will see too little savings for their own retirement.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In Budget 2023, we see that the Government has moved to strengthen retirement adequacy for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As part of our #EveryWorkerMatters conversation last month, together with my National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) colleagues and volunteers, I had the great opportunity to host a dialogue session at our NTUC premises for more than 100 employers, ex-offenders, Yellow Ribbon Singapore (YRSG), Singapore Prison Service (SPS) and New Charis Mission Friends.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is the first time that NTUC and the Labour Movement has engaged this community for a dialogue.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: On another occasion earlier this month, my team and I had an opportunity to engage a group of inmates at Changi Prison, as part of our #EveryWorkerMatters conversation, to share as well as hear their thoughts on jobs, skills, training, and employment and employability in general.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I applaud the work of YRSG and SPS, and for making our engagement possible, so that we can hear first-hand from this community as we forge a new workers' compact.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: The Tripartite Advisory on Mental Well-being at the Workplace was subsequently promulgated in November 2020, which included recommendations on after-hours work communication.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: In September 2021, the Alliance for Action on Work-life Harmony issued a policy template to help companies set clearer boundaries for after-hours work communication.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: What is MOM doing to encourage greater adoption?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: According to a 2023 report by the World Economic Forum (WEF), several countries – France, Belgium and Portugal – have legislated laws to allow employees to disconnect.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Portugal, for example, labels its work-life balance legislation the "right to rest", with companies of 10 or more staff facing penalties for contacting staff outside of set working hours.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: The same report also states that multinational corporations (MNCs), including a Belgian chemical company and an Italian bank, have signed multinational agreements with their European Work Councils to support workers' right to disconnect.

speaker: Mr Chairman
text: We will have our right to a break after Minister Tan See Leng's speech.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Unless the Members of the House want to exercise their right to disconnect.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Chairman, I thank our Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) Members of Parliament and the others, who have taken an active interest in MOM's work and spoken in support of our workers and our businesses.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our labour market posted strong growth last year.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Resident unemployment rates have recovered to pre-COVID-19 levels.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Resident wages also increased at a faster rate.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, we are at multiple crossroads, the uncertain global economic environment, global inflation and geopolitical challenges in the medium term, will weigh on the labour market going forward.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hear your concerns about what this means for you and how it will impact your jobs, especially for older workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But rest assured, we will journey with you every step of the way.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Whether you are in your early 20s or 30s, or whether you are in your mid-40s or your late-50s, we will empower you to find and work towards new opportunities.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But we need your help, your support to take the first step, to move forward, to improve your career prospects.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If you want a career change, you can be assured of the support we will provide you to upskill and to reskill.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If you fall out of employment, you can be assured that we will step in, to help you in your job search.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If your interest is in hands-on work, you can be assured of more opportunities to achieve and to be rewarded for the mastery of those skills.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And as you approach retirement, you can be assured that if you have worked and contributed consistently to your CPF, you will be able to meet your basic retirement needs in your golden years.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will leverage our continued economic growth to provide good jobs for you.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will improve and continue to improve, your employment outcomes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And even in the midst of this uncertainty, there are significant opportunities that we can continue to capitalise on.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I shared in my speech with the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) yesterday, on how we have a suite of programmes to promote talent development in our enterprises.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For those starting out in their careers, there is the Singapore Global Executive Programme (SGEP) to support fresh and recent graduates to pursue structured career progression pathways in high-growth companies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Global Ready Talent (GRT) programme also helps to build a talent pipeline by co-funding local young talent, to take on both local and overseas internships.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And for senior leaders of our promising SMEs, the Enterprise Leadership for Transformation (ELT) programme also helps them to develop their business strategies and leadership capabilities.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With the ever-changing economy, we need to continue to press on with economic transformation, to allow us to emerge stronger and to seize new opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We want you and we invite you to join us on this journey of transformation, and this is why we have been engaging Singaporeans to understand their aspirations, their angst about the economy, their anxieties about the economy and jobs under the Forward Singapore exercise.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is against this backdrop that MOM's priorities for this Committee of Supply (COS) will centre on three main themes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And last but not least, securing better workplaces with you.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: First, we will seize opportunities with Singaporeans by supporting them to improve their career prospects and their resilience, so that they will be empowered to take on good jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the same time, we will continue to be open to workers of the right calibre and in areas where we need them, so that our businesses can build the best team of local and foreign talents to grow.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our growth should also be inclusive and enable all segments of our workers to reap the economic benefits.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Hence, our second focus is to strengthen support for Singaporeans' retirement adequacy by enhancing the Central Provident Fund (CPF) system, so that they can have peace of mind in their golden years.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will also press on with our whole-of-society effort to provide greater support for platform workers, lower-wage workers and senior workers, by protecting their interests at work.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Senior Ministers of State Koh Poh Koon and Zaqy Mohamad will elaborate more on our efforts on this front in their respective speeches.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And finally, every one of us desires and deserves a fair opportunity to contribute and thrive at work, which brings me to our third focus, and that is to act collectively as one united society.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We must work in solidarity to secure safer, fairer and more progressive workplaces.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will continue to improve employment opportunities for women, for persons with disabilities and ex-offenders.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Minister of State Gan Siow Huang will elaborate on these in her speech.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will also continue with the efforts to improve safety in the work place and this will be covered by Senior Minister of State Zaqy in his speech as well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have a strong and vibrant economy that has shown its resilience through COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have an exciting vision to continue transforming our economy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To seize these opportunities, Singaporeans will need to stay open to new challenges and careers, and continuously upskill and equip themselves with future skills.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: MOM and the Government will be there with you every step of the way in this journey to improve your career prospects.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: During COVID-19, the Government stood up the National Jobs Council (NJC) to provide jobs and skill opportunities amidst a deep recession and a weak labour market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To complement the NJC's work, I set up the Jobs Taskforce in September 2021 with the specific goal of helping more locals enter new jobs in 10 key sectors such as information and communications, manufacturing and financial services.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The NJC and the Jobs Taskforce's achievements are a testament to the calibre and the agility of our local workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: MOM and WSG will continue to help Singaporeans pivot to new jobs and new careers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For example, WSG offers many Career Conversion Programmes (CCPs).

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: CCPs provide salary and training support to employers to reskill new hires and workers for new or redesigned jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In 2022, WSG launched several new CCPs for emerging jobs such as sustainability specialist, carbon project developer and customer intelligence analyst.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui asked how we are helping SMEs with hiring.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: SMEs can tap on the full suite of programmes offered by WSG.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In particular, WSG has designed the CCP for SME executives to meet the specific needs of SME hires.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This programme helps new employees acclimatise to an SME working environment.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Desmond Choo and Mr Patrick Tay would like to know how we can better support mature workers, including PMEs, in their employment and employability.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To provide more options for mature workers, WSG also offers SGUnited Mid-Career Pathways (SGUP), which provides full-time attachments with an allowance for those aged 40 and over.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: One such individual is Mr Noor Hashim, a 50-year-old who was previously an independent systems security auditor with a local security auditor company.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: He wanted to explore career options in the IT industry and he signed up for a six-month course under the SkillsFuture Career Transition Programme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Equipped with his new tech skills, Mr Hashim applied for the SGUP Programme on the MyCareersFuture website in September 2022.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: He landed an attachment role as an IT cloud and infrastructure specialist with the host organisation, Swiz Technologies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: During this six-month attachment, Swiz Technologies provided on-the-job training, including step-by-step demonstrations, to help him understand how to perform the job tasks of an IT cloud and infrastructure specialist.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I am glad to hear that based on his strong performance in the attachment programme, Mr Hashim will be converted to a full-time staff with Swiz Technologies this month.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ultimately, MOM is here to support Singaporeans' career aspirations.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: That is why we have been engaging and speaking to Singaporeans from all walks of life to understand their aspirations and their anxieties about the economy and jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These conversations under Forward Singapore have allowed us to come together to forge a new social compact.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: A social compact has to be mutually reinforcing, mutually consolidating.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is a two-way dialogue so that we can take in your responses and forge a new compact together.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have worked with the Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) to convene a Citizens' Panel on employment resilience and convene a group of citizens to discuss, to propose ideas to increase career mobility and to help workers to bounce back from setbacks such as unemployment.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Citizens' Panel will conclude its work by the end of March and I look forward to hearing their recommendations.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Having heard from many fellow Singaporeans so far, I hear a common theme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Whether you are starting out in your career, whether you are in your mid-career or in a later stage of your career, you aspire to improve your career prospects.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Better career health is key to helping our workers move up the career ladder, stay current and stay employable, or it facilitates them to be able to switch to a new job that can better match their skills and their interests.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I spoke about career health when I launched the Citizens' Panel last month.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Just like physical health, career health has three aspects.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We need to be more sensitised and to be more aware of our career prospects, relative to how the industry and the economy is growing or transforming.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Two, taking deliberate and purposeful actions to keep up our career health.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Information is only meaningful if we process it and we act on it.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This means taking pre-emptive and proactive steps to stay ahead of the competition and being ready to seize new opportunities when they come.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Three, how do we bounce back from setbacks?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Sometimes, in spite of whatever we do, curve balls will still come our way, out of the blue.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are thinking about how to give a stronger helping hand to help workers to bounce back stronger and better from setbacks.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But for this to work, workers need to keep up with their career health so that they are better prepared for setbacks and they are more ready to pick themselves up.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: One way MOM is helping to improve awareness on career health is through the Jobs Transformation Maps (JTMs).

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These JTMs provide detailed insights on the impact of technology and automation on jobs in each sector.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Prof Hoon Hian Teck and Mr Sharael Taha asked about how we ensure our workforce is globally competitive, including how to cope with threats arising from artificial intelligence (AI).

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These JTMs provide detailed insights on the impact of technology and automation on jobs in each sector.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The JTMs will empower you to take control of your career development and progression by giving you information on the critical skill sets you will need to stay relevant and competitive.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao, Ms Janet Ang and Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked how MOM can support our businesses to grow and cope with manpower shortages.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Fundamentally, to cope with the manpower crunch, businesses must continue to transform, to increase their productivity and to improve manpower efficiency.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Government remains committed to supporting businesses and workers to achieve this.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The JTMs will guide businesses on how they can transform their businesses and their jobs to remain competitive and resilient.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To find out more, you can access the JTMs on WSG's website.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For individuals, you can also find resources there to reskill, upskill or embark on career transitions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There will be more JTMs launched this year.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There is tremendous potential to harness data and AI to provide you more personalised jobs and skill insights.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This can help to improve job matching and allow you to better plan what next steps you can take – either to take a course to upskill, to make a career switch or to progress in your career.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have heard feedback that some of our workers prefer to explore job opportunities and skills upgrading at the same time as they are inter-related.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It uses data on skill adjacencies and job transitions in the labour market to help jobseekers to identify potential career opportunities, personalised based on their individual profiles and recommend suitable training programmes to help them achieve their career goals.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: CareersFinder is a new feature, which will be launched in a beta version, but it will become more powerful as the data grows.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will continue to enhance it over time to make it even more responsive to jobseekers' needs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Individuals who wish to find out more about CareersFinder can also register their interest via WSG's website.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Besides supporting workers to reskill and upskill, we need to build a more inclusive labour market that rewards mastery of skills in different areas.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our labour market must also provide multiple pathways to success to cater to different interests and inclinations.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our society has traditionally valued "head" work much more than "hands-on" work and "heart" work, contributing to occupational wage disparity.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Over time, if we are able to shift the prospects and perceptions of such jobs and offer attractive career pathways for skilled trades, we will be able to increase the number of locals in these roles in a sustainable way.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: More details on this initiative will be shared at a later date when the Forward Singapore exercise concludes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: A crucial aspect of how we create good opportunities for local workers is by having a vibrant, growing economy that is open to international investments, companies and talent.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Working alongside global talent and in top companies means locals have access to more opportunities to take on challenging assignments and to move up in their careers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This also creates more opportunities for other companies in the ecosystem and in turn creates more good jobs for Singaporeans at every level of the workforce, creating a virtuous cycle.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas asked about how we will continue to attract top talent to Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This was a highly targeted enhancement to attract top talent in diverse fields so that we can keep ahead of the competition.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Yuki Yasui is the managing director of the Asia Pacific network at the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero, a global coalition of leading financial institutions committed to accelerating the decarbonisation of the economy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Yasui plays a key role in driving decarbonisation in Singapore, including helping financial institutions draw up their net-zero transition plans and mobilising finance to support decarbonisation efforts in key industry sectors such as energy, cement and steel.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We also have Prof Rachel Watson, who joined A*STAR this month as the Executive Director of the A*STAR Skin Research Labs and the Skin Research Institute of Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Through her leadership, she will catalyse our local community of research scientists, academics and industry professionals to tackle complex challenges in skin disease and skin health for the benefit of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We look forward to the valuable contributions that our ONE Pass holders will bring and the opportunities that they will create for Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As Mr Raj Joshua Thomas, Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Mr Yip Hon Weng highlighted, it is key for our foreign workforce to complement our local workforce to drive our local economy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We would also like to assure Mr Yip that MOM collaborates closely with agencies such as MTI and MND to ensure that our economic growth is sustainable, as we maintain a balance between our various objectives.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the last Committee of Supply (COS) debate, I announced significant changes to our foreign workforce policies to strengthen the complementarity of our foreign workforce.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our focus has been on implementing these changes well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Allow me to give you a quick update.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To ensure that foreigners coming in on these passes are of the right calibre, we have benchmarked the cost of hiring an Employment Pass and S Pass holder to the wages of the top one-third of local Professionals, Managers, Executives and Technicians (PMETs) and the local Associate Professionals and Technicians (APTs) respectively.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With these clear benchmarks, employers can expect regular and predictable adjustments to the EP and S Pass qualifying salaries and levies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The qualifying salary for older S Pass holders will be higher, given that local APT wages rise with age.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Employers will be able to find these details on the MOM website.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: COMPASS incentivises firms to strengthen their local workforce, complemented by a high quality and diverse foreign workforce.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have released details on the four foundational criteria progressively over the past one year.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Firms now have access to a Workforce Insights Tool on MyMOMPortal, where they can see how they fare on the firm-level criteria of COMPASS and benchmark their performance to industry peers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members may recall that under the COMPASS framework, applicants can score points under Criterion 2 on "Qualifications".

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Today, employers are already responsible for ensuring the authenticity of their candidate's qualifications before hiring.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To safeguard against gaming by submitting fraudulent educational qualifications, employers who wish to score points under Criterion 2 on qualifications, will be required to submit verification proof for qualifications declared on the EP application.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have consulted tripartite partners as well as industry associations and we will implement this new process in September 2023 together with COMPASS.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will share more details in due course.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Rest assured we will ensure smooth implementation and we will minimise disruptions to employers' hiring process.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will be releasing further details on the two bonus criteria, the Skills Bonus (Criterion 5) and the Strategic Economic Priorities Bonus (Criterion 6) later this month.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Applicants meeting the respective criteria will earn bonus points towards their total COMPASS score.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Skills Bonus is accorded to EP applicants in occupations on the Shortage Occupation List (SOL).

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The SOL identifies occupations requiring niche and highly specialised skills in short supply within our workforce and which are critical to sustaining investments in both key growth or strategic priority areas.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Gerald Giam asked for an update on the occupations expected to be included in the SOL.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: MOM, in consultation with sector agencies, is finalising the inaugural SOL.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: One key consideration is ensuring that sector agencies have worked with industry to put in place plans to develop the local pipeline for these good jobs, including working with our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) to equip graduates with the necessary skills, as well as developing and upskilling those already in the sector or adjacent roles.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Where relevant, the sector agencies also obtained input from industry partners and unions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This ensures that the SOL is responsive to industry developments while preserving enough certainty and runway for businesses.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Strategic Economic Priorities (SEP) Bonus was designed together with MTI and participating economic agencies as well as the Labour Movement, NTUC.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is a highly selective bonus which supports firms that are contributing to Singapore's strategic economic priorities through ambitious investment, innovation, internationalisation, or company and workforce transformation activities.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Economic agencies will work with firms receiving the SEP Bonus to pursue these needle-moving economic priorities and who are able to demonstrate their commitment to developing our local workforce.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: NTUC will work with firms on company and workforce transformation efforts, for example, by establishing Company Training Committees (CTCs) to chart out worker upskilling plans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Firms receiving the SEP bonus would be expected to maintain healthy workforce profiles on nationality diversity and local PMET employment, as a condition for renewal.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked for an update on the Fair Consideration Framework (FCF).

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Since 2016, MOM has engaged a total of more than 1,800 employers under the FCF.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As I announced during last year's COS debate, COMPASS builds on our current efforts under the FCF, by applying firm-related attributes at the point of application.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Once COMPASS is rolled out, the FCF Watchlist will be re-purposed to focus on firms scoring poorly on the firm-related attributes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP) will conduct workshops for these firms to highlight measures that firms can take to improve their hiring practices.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Tay also asked to publish the list of companies with weak workforce profiles.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I have explained before that doing so will affect the business of these firms and potentially hinder their effort to improve their practices.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, instead, our approach is to have TAFEP work with them to improve their practices.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Rest assured that MOM will continue to take fair consideration seriously and I will elaborate on our efforts under the Workplace Fairness Legislation in the second part of my speech.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Desmond Choo and Mr Cheng Hsing Yao have also suggested calibrating our foreign workforce policies further to address issues such as insufficient locals in certain sectors, or in anticipation of our ageing population.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Sectors such as construction and process have higher foreign worker quotas, as we recognise that fewer locals join these sectors and we exercise flexibilities to better support essential services like healthcare and the cleaning of public housing.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our moves announced last year also took on a more nuanced and targeted approach.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For instance, businesses that contribute to our strategic economic priorities can tap on the Manpower for Strategic Economic Priorities (M-SEP) scheme to access additional quotas.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Another example is the Non-Traditional Source (NTS) Occupation List.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members would recall that I announced this last year to allow employers in the Services and Manufacturing sectors to hire Work Permit Holders from NTS countries for seven occupational types.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The sub-quota guards against over-reliance on NTS workers and ensures that employers diversify their workforce.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The salary criterion safeguards against cheap-sourcing and incentivises employers to hire higher-skilled or more experienced workers from these source countries.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Employers who are putting their existing NTS S Pass holders on Work Permits will have no trouble meeting the salary criterion.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: MOM will continue to work closely with the agencies and industries to review the NTS Occupation List from time to time.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members of the House, our growth must also be inclusive so as to enable all segments of our workers to reap the benefits.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will therefore also further strengthen our support for you.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon and Senior Minister of State Zaqy will elaborate further on how we intend to strengthen protection and support for Platform Workers, lower-wage workers, senior workers and migrant workers in their speeches.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Even as we were tackling the immediate challenges of the pandemic, we maintained a steady focus on our longer-term objective of enhancing our workers' retirement adequacy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Abdul Samad and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked for an update on the retirement adequacy of Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We recognise that the number of retiree households has been increasing and thus have been enhancing the CPF system, especially for the vulnerable segments who may require further support, including our senior workers and lower-wage workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Over the last decade, the proportion of active CPF members attaining their cohort Basic Retirement Sum (BRS) at age 55 has improved from about five in 10 to almost seven in 10 today.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We expect this number to increase to about eight in 10 in 2027.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman and Mr Yip Hon Weng spoke in favour of enhancing the employability of seniors.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: That is an important strategy to help CPF members continue to build up their retirement nest egg through employment even after age 55.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Senior Minister of State Koh will be elaborating more on our efforts in supporting the retirement adequacy for senior workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Together with the enhanced WIS, our efforts in uplifting the wages of lower-wage workers will help them save more for their retirement.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Senior Minister of State Zaqy will share more details later.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For seniors who require further support for their retirement, CPF payouts are one of many sources of retirement income.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Seniors may also receive targeted support from the Government through schemes such as ComCare and the Silver Support Scheme, which we enhanced in 2011.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Further, at Budget 2023, the Government announced enhancements to the Assurance Package and permanent GST Voucher scheme, to help Singaporeans tide through this period of higher inflation and to cushion the impact of the GST rate increase.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In addition, seniors may also tap on their accumulated private savings, if available.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If not, they may receive additional support from the community such as through charities.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As you can tell, we are building from a position of strength.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are doing more to enhance the CPF system.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Louis Chua asked for a review of the interest rates of the CPF Ordinary Account (OA).

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are aware that the OA pegged rate has remained relatively stable amidst the current elevated interest rate environment while the yields of other market instruments of comparable risk and duration have increased.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Even as we study this, I should point out that during the low interest-rate environment of the last decade, we have paid a fair interest rate.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The 2.5% floor for the OA has exceeded the pegged rate for over 20 years, even when market interest rates were low, such as during the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked if we intend to revise the interest rates as market interest rates crossed 4% in 2023.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This helps to smoothen the short-term market fluctuations on the interest rates.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If the pegged rate exceeds the floor rate of 4%, members will correspondingly earn the higher interest rate on their CPF savings.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members aged 55 and above receive 2% extra interest on the first $30,000 of combined CPF balances and 1% on the next $30,000.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Louis Chua also asked if the CPF Investment Scheme (CPFIS) could be made more comprehensive and if there could be more direct means by which members can earn higher investment returns other than via CPFIS.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Chua had raised similar points last year.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With the benefit of hindsight, it will always appear easy to achieve a higher rate of returns.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But we have said before, that higher returns also come with higher risk and a greater potential for losses.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Today, CPF members can invest in a diverse range of products, including exchange-traded funds (ETFs), shares and gold products.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members who prefer not to take any risks with their retirement savings already enjoy risk-free interest rates of up to 6% per annum on their CPF savings, where investment risk is entirely borne by the Government.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I would also like to thank Mr Pritam Singh for his suggestion during the recent Budget debate to reallocate a greater proportion of CPF contributions for younger members to their SA.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This was raised by Miss Cheryl Chan during the CPF (Amendment) Bill in 2021 and by Mr Saktiandi Supaat during his cut.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are considering this idea and are very glad that Members have come out to support it.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I sincerely hope that if and when we do eventually put up this proposal, the Workers' Party (WP) would be in full support of it.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This will be done in phases, starting with $300 this year, to allow employers and employees to adjust to the changes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There will be no change to the annual salary ceiling at $102,000.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: An example of a worker who is supportive of the higher salary ceiling is Mr Fadzli Jamil.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: He is 38 years old and is the associate dean in the School of 3D Design at the Nanyang Academy of Fine Arts (NAFA).

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Of course, for each year, should he choose to defer the start of his payouts, his monthly payouts will increase further by up to 7%.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Employers' business costs are also likely to remain manageable as the increases are spread out over four years.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The additional business cost impact is around half a billion per annum because not all workers are affected by the maximum increase of $2,000.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As part of the Forward Singapore exercise, we are taking a deeper look at what should be done to improve the retirement adequacy of Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is especially relevant with the greater economic uncertainties amidst global challenges, at least in the medium term.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For the group that are in their 50s and early-60s today, they have a limited runway to work and save.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will also do more for our younger and middle-aged workers and the Pioneer and Merdeka Generation seniors, many of whom are retirees.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I believe that if we journey through the crossroads together, we will be able to align the crossroads and forge a new social compact, one where the Government, employers and our fellow Singaporeans can work together to improve career prospects, strengthen retirement adequacy and bring fair levels of reward and respect for all forms of work.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is one where no worker is left behind as Singapore progresses.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With improved career health, you will be able to stay ahead of technological trends and seize many new job opportunities within and beyond your sector.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In your golden years, we will support you such that you will be able to have a peace of mind if you have worked and you have contributed consistently to your CPF.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I look forward to having more conversations with you and working together to create an inclusive society abundant and brimming with opportunities.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I will share more about securing better workplaces with you in the next segment of my speech.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.00 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.38 pm until 4.00 pm.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Mr Chairman, earlier, the Minister for Manpower outlined how the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) will strengthen our efforts to uplift lower-wage workers and improve workplace safety.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: In my speech, I will elaborate on: (a) tripartite progress in implementing Progressive Wage measures; (b) measures to further support and uplift lower-wage workers; and (c) Heightened Safety Period (HSP) measures to strengthen workplace safety and health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I will also elaborate on our efforts in strengthening human resources (HR) capabilities to support businesses, workforce and workplace transformation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: PWMs and other tripartite efforts have borne fruit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This means that as costs of living rose, the incomes of lower-wage workers rose even more.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: More importantly, we are narrowing the income gap between lower-wage workers and the median worker.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We will continue our efforts to support lower-wage workers so that they achieve stronger wage outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Allow me to update on the progress that tripartite partners have made.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Members may also access the handout through the SG Parl MP mobile app.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: At the same time, we also introduced the retail PWM, and extended existing cleaning, security and landscape PWMs to in-house workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In January, we launched the Progressive Wage Mark accreditation scheme.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Starting from today, we embark on another milestone.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: PWMs will continue to set the pace for wage increases for lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Amidst a tight labour market, lower-wage workers who are not directly covered by Progressive Wages should still see meaningful wage increases, as employers will have to adjust according to market forces to attract and retain workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Chairman, with almost all PWMs implemented, our attention is now focused on ensuring that employers understand the requirements and comply with them.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Employers must pay workers the right PWM wage based on the PWM job role.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We recognise that the PWM requirements are new for many employers and employers need time to understand them and make necessary HR or operational changes to comply.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Hence, for new PWMs implemented since last September, MOM allowed a run-in period of six months, where we invested time to educate employers and workers on the requirements.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: After the run-in period, employers who are found to be non-compliant may face suspension of their Work Pass privileges.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Some Members such as Mr Raj Joshua Thomas and Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman asked how PWM might affect employers' manpower deployment or workforce restructuring plans.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Tripartite partners recognise that employers may need to adjust manpower deployment plans or their workforce structure, based on their operating environment.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: However, when there is a need to make adjustments, employers should act in accordance with well-established tripartite advisories, such as the Tripartite Advisory on Managing Excess Manpower (TAMEM).

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Employers should engage and discuss with unions and employees and reach an agreement before implementing any measures.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Most importantly, employers should also pay special attention to minimise the impact of any measure on our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These principles should be adhered to, with or without PWM.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I also agree with Ms Yeo Wan Ling and Mr Xie Yao Quan that consumers and service buyers also play an important role in our whole-of-society effort to support and uplift lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In January, the Government launched the Progressive Wage Mark, or PW Mark, to help consumers and service buyers more easily identify firms that are paying Progressive Wages and support them.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Employers who also adopt the Tripartite Standard on Advancing Well-Being of Lower-Wage Workers will be accredited with the Progressive Wage Mark Plus.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These are employers who not only pay progressive wages, but also implement other measures that support lower-wage workers, such as providing for rest areas.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Government will take the lead in this effort and help further the adoption of the Progressive Wage Mark.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For new tenders called from today onwards, the Government will require eligible suppliers and subcontractors to be accredited with the Progressive Wage Mark for the duration of the contract period.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: From 1 March next year, we will extend this requirement to quotations as well.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This will cover the slew of tenders and quotations for procurement by the Government.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Uplifting lower-wage workers is our collective responsibility as a society.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I strongly encourage employers to do their part by paying progressive wages and apply for the Progressive Wage Mark or Progressive Wage Mark Plus.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Consumers and service buyers can show their support and solidarity with our lower-wage workers by purchasing from Progressive Wage Mark-accredited companies.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Chairman, the PWMs have set strong wage growth targets, on average of about 8% year-on-year.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To support wage growth of our lower-wage workers, while balancing the uncertain economic conditions facing employers, we will continue to provide strong support to employers in adjusting to Progressive Wage measures.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Last year, the Government introduced the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme (PWCS) to help employers adjust to the new Progressive Wage and LQS requirements, and other voluntary wage increases for lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Deputy Prime Minister announced in his Budget Statement for FY2023 that the Government will increase our PWCS co-funding share for wage increases given this year, in 2023.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Similar to the enhancement made last year, the Government will co-fund up to 75% of wage increases for eligible lower-wage workers, including those not covered by our Progressive Wage moves.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: All in all, these PWCS enhancements will offset a significant proportion of immediate cost pressures on employers arising from our efforts to uplift lower-wage workers and mitigate cost transfer to consumers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I urge employers to take the opportunity to accelerate their business transformation plans so that we can improve productivity, upskill our workers, and ensure that we can continue to close the income gap sustainably over the long term.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Workfare is one of the key pillars of Government's support for our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Workfare Skills Support Scheme (WSS) is an important scheme that supports the upskilling of lower-wage workers, to improve their employability and earnings.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Under WSS, employers who send lower-wage workers for training receive an Absentee Payroll subsidy of 95% of their workers' basic hourly wage.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Employees who self-sponsor their training will receive a training allowance, which offsets their opportunity costs of training.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: WSS has been successful in supporting lower-wage workers in achieving more impactful employment outcomes.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is why we will be enhancing WSS from July this year.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In addition, as lower-wage workers who achieve Full Qualifications through WSS are more likely to earn higher wages, we will raise the Training Commitment Award for Full Qualifications from $500 to $800, to encourage more lower-wage workers to undertake deeper and more sustained training.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Last year, the Government announced significant enhancements to the Workfare Income Supplement Scheme (WIS) which have taken effect from January 2023.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The enhancements increased coverage by extending Workfare to those aged 30 to 34 years, from 35 years and older previously, as well as raising the qualifying monthly income cap to $2,500 from $2,300 previously.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In addition, Workfare payments have been increased to up to $4,200 per year, from up to $4,000 previously – that is about $350 a month.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: All persons with disabilities (PwDs) will also qualify for the highest Workfare payment tier of up to $4,200, regardless of age.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Collectively, the Progressive Wage moves, WSS and WIS strengthen our support for our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Chairman, moving on to workplace safety and health (WSH).

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Melvin Yong have asked about the Government's efforts to reduce workplace fatalities and injuries and instilling a stronger safe operations culture.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: In 2022, MOM introduced various measures to address the spate of workplace fatalities.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We ended 2022 with a total of 46 workplace fatalities and a fatality rate of 1.3 per 100,000 workers, which was higher than the pre-COVID-19-pandemic rates of 1.1 in 2019 and 1.2 in 2018.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The number of workplace fatalities would have been higher without the implementation of the Heightened Safety Period (HSP) measures last September.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The average number of fatalities per month reduced from 4.5 in January to August 2022, before HSP, to 2.5 in September to December 2022 during HSP.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The average of 2.5 fatalities per month brings the annualised fatality rate to 0.8 per 100,000, which is below our WSH2028 target of 1.0 and much lower compared to 1.5 before HSP.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: What this suggests is that the industry can keep the fatality numbers low if we put our hearts and minds to it.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We also monitor major injuries closely as these reflect persistent safety lapses and have debilitating effects.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The average monthly major injuries worsened from 49.1 before HSP to 55.3 during HSP.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But it is not all doom and gloom because we found that the impact of HSP was uneven across sectors.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: There are major injuries that have high probability of fatalities and there are also major injuries like slips, trips and falls which have low probability of fatality.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Although the monthly average fatal and major injuries in the construction sector showed the most improvement, the monthly average fatal and major injuries worsened for the manufacturing sector.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, when the rate for the construction sector came down, that also resulted in fewer fatalities because major injuries there tend to be more fatal.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We also monitored and saw that for transportation and storage, the monthly average fatal injuries remained the same, while major injuries worsened.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Nonetheless, this suggested that more targeted sectoral measures were needed.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, to Members' questions as to what we are doing differently?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As part of our HSP measures, we stood up the Multi-Agency Workplace Safety Taskforce, which comprises lead agencies of the sectors that contributed most of the fatal and major injuries.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This aims to study additional broad-based, and at the same time, sectoral measures that should be implemented, by looking into the different risk profile and impact of HSP in each sector.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We also convened the International Advisory Panel on Workplace Safety and Health (WSH) in January 2023.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: MOM and our sector agency partners will also take into account their recommendations.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, it is both MOM at the broad-based level and we also have agencies involved at the sectoral level.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It is important for corporate senior leadership to take charge and be accountable for workplace safety and health.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Their influence and control over workplace resources and priorities drive the safety culture in their organisations.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Under the Workplace Safety and Health Act, they are liable for ensuring their workers' safety and health.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The approved Code of Practice for Company Directors' WSH Duties gazetted last October provides practical guidance on how they may fulfil their legal WSH obligations.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As part of the HSP extension, MOM introduced additional measures to strengthen WSH ownership among company leaders.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, it is always continuous learning for them too.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To Mr Leon Perera's question earlier about whistle-blowing, under the WSH Act today, there are already existing protections for whistle-blowers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To dismiss them will be a WSH contravention and we will take action.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I can assure the Member that MOM will facilitate the change of employers if there is a reason to and we will do so if you have any specific cases you want to raise to us.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To Mr Melvin Yong's query, HSP was a useful wake up call to all employers and workers to be extra vigilant.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The improvements seen during HSP demonstrate that safer workplaces are possible.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As Mr Christopher de Souza and Dr Wan Rizal said, everyone must play our part to uplift workplace safety and health so that our workers can have a peace of mind when they return home safely to their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Starting with the top management, company directors and CEOs must set the culture of their organisations where safety consciousness is integrated in all of its operations and provide a safe work environment with appropriate and adequate training for their workers, supported by supervisors and safety professionals.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Workers themselves are responsible for following safe work procedures to ensure their own safety and that of others in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: They should report all unsafe practices to their supervisors and if their concerns are not addressed, they should alert MOM or their union representatives.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Union leaders should join company management for walkabouts to strengthen top management's commitment to their workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Members of the public can also be our "eyes on the ground" by reporting unsafe practices to MOM.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For example, you may report workers who are working at height without safety harnesses.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: You can do so via MOM's website or hotline or the QR code found on project signboards.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: MOM will continue to work with companies, industry associations and workers to build a stronger workplace safety and health culture.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Together, we can get back on track with our Workplace Safety and Health 2028 mission to reduce the fatal injury rate to below one per 100,000 workers and join just four countries in the OECD that have achieved this fatality rate.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The reason why I say that this is a target is because there are very few countries that can achieve this and we are setting very high standards for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Beyond workplace safety, promoting physical health at workplaces is also important.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Leon Perera asked about service staff having the right to sit.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The Employment Act establishes some rules on working hours to protect employees' well-being.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For example, employees covered under Part 4 of the Act should have at least one rest break for every six consecutive hours of work.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Besides legislation, the Government also promotes the provision of proper rest areas for employees.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We are mindful of the wide range of work settings for which it will not be appropriate to impose excessive or overly prescriptive regulations.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Nonetheless, we are open to discussing with tripartite partners and industry associations on possible tripartite guidance on best practices for employers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We encourage all employers to provide adequate rest and welfare for all staff, including service staff, and tap on the Workcare Grant should they require support to do so.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It is only right for employers to provide their staff with a conducive work environment.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Staff will also be motivated and engaged as a result.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Chairman, let me also share our efforts to strengthen HR capabilities.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Post-pandemic, a strong HR is a critical enabler of business and workforce transformation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: From helping businesses attract the right talent to implementing fair and inclusive employment practices, HR will play an integral role.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We will do more to support and build up the capabilities of our HR workforce.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: IHRP is a tripartite organisation that supports the professional development of aspiring and existing HR professionals.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: All certified HR professionals join a vibrant community which provides access to an extensive professional network and resources.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: These playbooks are developed with master or senior HR professionals to provide the community with curated best practices and tools that they can adopt in their organisations to respond to workforce challenges.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To date, IHRP has produced seven such books, covering important issues such as the emergence of hybrid workplaces, digital transformation and the promotion of mental well-being.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We encourage firms and company HR leaders to adopt them.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This suggests that businesses and HR professionals see value in certification.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: While we echo Mr Patrick Tay's call to have more HR professionals certified, we have no plans to make it mandatory at this point.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We are mindful of imposing regulatory costs on businesses.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Besides, good HR practices apply to all companies, whether or not they hire foreign manpower.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Nevertheless, I agree with the Member that besides HR, People Managers also play a critical role in supporting good human capital practices.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To this end, MOM will work with IHRP and its partners on the suggestion to better equip People Managers with requisite HR knowledge and progressive practices.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Besides IHRP certification, we agree with Mr Edward Chia that HR professionals also need to continually update their skills and hone their expertise.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Continuous professional development is a key part of being a certified HR professional.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: HR professionals can take up IHRP skills badges in emerging areas such as strategic workforce planning and talent management.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: IHRP has been appointed by SkillsFuture Singapore as a Skills Development Partner (SDP).

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: MOM is working with IHRP to more responsively identify skills gaps and develop skills-based credentialling pathways for HR professionals.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Professionalising our HR workforce and equipping them with relevant skills and mindsets is necessary but insufficient in itself.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Enterprises must make use of these highly skilled HR professionals to transform their HR capabilities.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This will set out a roadmap for MOM to work together with sector agencies, the industry and the unions to spur HR transformation and build a future-ready HR workforce.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Mr Chairman, may I just cover the last bit in Malay, please?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: (In Malay):   Mr Chairman, as stated by the Minister for Manpower, the Government is committed to ensuring that our workforce policies provide more opportunities for all.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Helping lower-wage workers has always been one of MOM's priorities.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Since the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) was introduced more than 10 years ago, it has contributed significantly to raising wages and supporting the lives of our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This not only covers workers in the cleaning, security, landscape as well as lift and escalator maintenance, but also new sectors such as food services, retail, waste management and occupations such as administrators and drivers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Workers in these sectors will enjoy significant wage increases and be given training opportunities as well as career progression.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For example, we can expect cleaners to get at least $2,420 by 2028, while security officers will get $3,530 by 2028.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: All other local workers working with companies employing foreign workers will also be paid at least the Local Qualifying Salary (LQS) amount of $1,400 monthly.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: On the whole, these measures will support our goal of bridging the wage gap further between lower- and middle-income workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: At the same time, workers must play their part in training and skills upgrading.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: (In English): Chairman, the Government is committed to strengthening the support of our lower-wage workers and partnering employers to improve workplace safety.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We must all do our part for a more inclusive and cohesive society, where everyone enjoys the fruits of growth and no worker is left behind as Singapore progresses.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Society must also continue to appreciate and respect workers in all trades.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Chairman, in today's challenging economic climate, senior workers and platform workers require stronger safety nets for their housing and retirement needs and better protections for their livelihoods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The proportion of Self-Employed Persons (SEPs) has remained steady at about 8% to 10% of the resident workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: However, with the rise of platform-enabled work, platform workers have become a fast-growing group of SEPs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Several Members, including Ms Hazel Poa, Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Ms Yeo Wan Ling, highlighted the need to reduce the risks that platform workers face during the course of their work and made suggestions on how to better support them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Indeed, the Government recognises the precarious nature of platform work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Other countries are also looking at ways to protect their Platform Workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In Spain, the Government passed the Riders’ Law in 2022 that recognises food delivery riders working for digital platforms as employees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The US Labour Department proposed a rule that would make it easier for platform workers to be considered as employees, with the same access to benefits and federal labour protections.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: While the UK has no Platform Worker-specific legislation, their courts have ruled on the status of Platform Workers’ status using the case law approach.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Here in Singapore, instead of simply designating Platform Workers as employees or leaving it to the Courts to decide on a matter of policy, we have taken a carefully considered Tripartite approach to provide three specific areas of legislated protections for our Platform Workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Over the course of a wide-ranging segment of engagements by the Advisory Committee that lasted for over a year, Platform Workers and Platform Companies emphasised that the flexible nature of platform work was a key feature of the ecosystem that should be preserved.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Platform Workers desire the flexibility to choose when and how much they want to work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Platform Companies need the flexibility to efficiently match the supply and demand of labour to meet consumer needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Simply designating Platform Workers as employees would constrain this flexibility and autonomy that both the company and the workers desire.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Our approach strengthens the protections for Platform Workers while retaining the advantages of platform work, so that the platform system can remain sustainable in the longer term.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Since the Government’s acceptance of the recommendations, we have made good progress working through complex issues with our key stakeholders, including tripartite partners, Platform Workers and Platform Companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We started a new Platform Workers Work Injury Compensation Implementation Network (PWIN) to look into how the existing Work Injury Compensation system for employees can be adapted to reap its benefits, such as adequate coverage and expeditious claims, while taking into consideration the unique nature of the platform work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Ms Hazel Poa and Ms Yeo Wan Ling spoke about the need to address concerns on the housing and retirement needs of Platform Workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In principle, Platform Workers of the same age and income level as employees should be able to achieve a similar level of retirement adequacy through their CPF savings, if they have worked for the same number of years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This will help Platform Workers build up their savings in their CPF Ordinary and Special Accounts, on top of their MediSave Accounts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It will be mandatory for the cohort of Platform Workers below 30 years old in the year of implementation, meaning those born in or after 1995.
