speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In fact, a study by the Institute for Policy Studies (IPS) found that younger Platform Workers expressed stronger preference for additional CPF contributions to help meet their housing needs, as they were more likely to have housing obligations, or have plans to buy a house.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: One of the Platform Workers IPS spoke to as part of their studies last year was Hamza.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: He had to fork out a large amount of cash for his new house just when he first switched to private hire driving.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This caught him off guard and he felt it would have been less of a concern for him if he had a job that provided CPF contributions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Once the Committee’s recommendations on CPF have been implemented, Platform Workers like Hamza will be able to tap on the additional CPF contributions to the Ordinary Account to pay for their housing loans instead of using cash.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We hope that this will help to relieve the stress felt by many younger Platform Workers on servicing their housing loans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Older Platform Workers born before 1995 can opt in for CPF contributions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To Ms Hazel Poa’s question, the decision to opt in would not be reversible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Platform Workers today have a concession to opt in for CPF, which is a choice that employees do not have.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Staying committed to these CPF contributions and allowing the earnings to accumulate interest over time is what will help these workers develop housing and retirement adequacy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Furthermore, in discussions with Platform Companies, it would be complex and add to compliance cost if Platform Workers are allowed to opt out after opting in.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is the feedback we get from the implementation discussions we have with these companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We strongly recommend that older cohorts of Platform Workers opt in, as they can similarly benefit from having additional contributions by the Platform Companies to build up their retirement nest egg.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Like employees, Platform Workers who earn between $50 and $500 a month will also be able to receive CPF contributions from the Platform Companies without having to make CPF contributions on their own.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Companies, workers and consumers all recognised the need for more protections for Platform Workers during our engagements with them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But there were concerns about the cost impact of these recommendations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This will help to address their concerns and smoothen the transition.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Platform Workers are likely to see an increase in their total earnings after factoring in additional CPF contributions from Platform Companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But at the same time, I know that some Platform Workers are concerned about the impact of the CPF changes on their take-home pay.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is why we will provide transitional support targeted at the lower-income Platform Workers earning up to $2,500 a month who see an increase in their CPF contribution rates, as Deputy Prime Minister announced during the Budget.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I hope this addresses the concerns from Ms Hazel Poa, Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Ms Yeo Wan Ling.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In addition, Platform Workers who align their CPF contributions to employees earlier will receive stronger support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The offset will taper down gradually over the next three years of the phase-in period for CPF contribution.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And to Mr Liang Eng Hwa’s appeal for the Government to support Platform Workers with reemployment and reskilling, I want to assure him that regardless of how long Platform Workers decide to stay in platform work, we will support those who wish to transit to other sectors, through the Career Conversion Programmes (CCPs) which provide salary and training support to employers to reskill new workers, and the Jobs and Skills Centres, which provide career coaching and advice, both of which Minister had mentioned earlier on in his speech.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Their increase in Workfare payments will be fully in cash.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: From the second half of 2024, all Platform Workers eligible for WIS will also start to receive monthly instead of yearly WIS payments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will be able to do so by then, as Platform Workers’ CPF contributions will be made more regularly, instead of the current arrangements in which they receive WIS only on a yearly basis after they declare their Net Trade Income at the end of each year and made the required MediSave contributions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, as a result of a more regular contribution, we will be able to have a mechanism to give WIS more regularly as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The above measures will mitigate the concerns in take-home pay while ensuring Platform Workers receive a significant boost to their retirement savings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Take for example a median income Platform Worker who turns 30 in 2024 and opts in from the start for the CPF contributions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Based on our estimates, he can use about $450,000 in CPF savings by age 65 for his housing and retirement needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In my engagements with Platform Workers, they also raised concerns about Platform Companies discriminating against those who opted for CPF, by assigning less jobs to them, a point that some Members raised as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Tripartite Committee on Workplace Fairness has, in its recently released interim report, recommended that the Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices (TGFEP) be enhanced to provide clarity that intermediaries, including Platform Companies, should treat workers fairly, including contracted workers, like Platform Workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: What this means is that Platform Companies must not discriminate when assigning work and MOM will investigate any unfair practices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, this is the assurance we want to give to all the workers out there if you have this concern.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: While the impact of discrimination on earnings has been top of mind for many Platform Workers, in my engagements with them, many also raised concerns about issues such as working conditions, earnings, safety at work and timely dispute resolution with customers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: A prevalent sentiment amongst many of them, is that they are often not accorded due recognition on their feedback and concerns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Addressing these issues requires a balanced relationship between the Platform Workers and the Platform Companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Platform Workers should be provided a clear representative voice to surface their concerns to maintain industrial peace and harmony within the platform ecosystem.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This relationship must be premised on Singapore’s unique approach of tripartism that encourages consultation, open communication and conciliation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The ability for Platform Workers to represent themselves and negotiate for their interests is critical as the industry continues to evolve and business models continue to change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In other countries like the UK and Spain for instance, unions have entered into collective agreements with platform companies to negotiate better working conditions, in areas such as earnings, grievance handling and safety.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In Singapore, currently, there are associations that represent these Platform Workers, but they are not formally recognised within our industrial relations framework and therefore they lack the mandate to negotiate on their behalf.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: While other jurisdictions have taken the approach of allowing platform workers to unionise in the same way that employees do, we recognise that the platform sector is distinct from traditional employment sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For instance, unlike employees, Platform Workers multi-home on different App platforms and are more geographically dispersed and transient in the time that they use to work or receive work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This has implications on how they can organise themselves and how their representatives are chosen.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Business models can evolve very rapidly and this has implications on what both parties can negotiate on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Therefore, the representation framework has to be suited to the needs and characteristics of the platform sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The TWG was designed as an avenue for tripartite partners to co-create this framework.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Through this process, they develop shared ownership of the eventual framework but more importantly, they build mutual trust.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is fundamental to fostering harmonious industrial relations in the platform space, which has been a core strength in our Singapore’s labour landscape.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And we need to cultivate this same spirit of tripartism in the platform ecosystem.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Third, stakeholders agree that the representation framework should be flexible enough such that individual representatives of Platform Workers and Platform Companies have the maximum space to negotiate and find win-win outcomes that are fair to all parties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Exercising good sense and goodwill is key to this endeavour.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will provide further updates once the TWG has completed its work in a few months.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Chairman, strengthening protections for platform workers will require a whole-of-community effort.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These decisive moves are necessary for a more inclusive society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Everyone has a part to play to safeguard the interests of platform workers today so that they can be better prepared in the face of future economic uncertainties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Platform workers themselves will need to set aside savings for their component of CPF contributions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: They will in turn receive contributions from platform companies who tap on them for labour.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Singaporeans, as consumers, are willing to bear some increases in costs to platform services, knowing that their contributions will make a difference to enhance protections for platform workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Government will implement the recommendations in stages over the next few years and provide transitional support to allay the impact to the platform ecosystem and to consumers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is how we build a social compact and engender a more inclusive society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As Ms Denise Phua and Mr Saktiandi Supaat pointed out, there are other groups of SEPs who have greater control over their own business models and are not subject to similar levels of management control as platform workers, but who also face unique challenges over the course of their work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will continue to review if there is a need to go beyond encouraging SEPs to make voluntary contributions to their CPF accounts, taking into account the needs and challenges of SEPs as well as the nature and context of their work arrangements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As a diverse group with different needs, support to SEPs is usually tailored to the needs of the sectors they function in.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Specific to Ms Denise Phua's question on the support for arts and sports SEPs, the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY) will share more about their initiatives to better support their professional needs in their Committee of Supply (COS) debates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Next, I would like to focus on our efforts to support our mature workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With better health and life expectancy, more seniors are capable of remaining in productive employment and supporting their own retirement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Hence, over the last few years, we have put in place structures and policies to support senior workers who wish to work longer to do so and to achieve stronger retirement adequacy as they do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Through these efforts, our senior resident employment rate has remained healthy and even increased despite the economic turbulence in the past few years of the pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This places our employment rate at 11th and fourth respectively when compared with the OECD countries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is comparable to other Asian countries such as South Korea.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will seize this momentum and continue to strengthen support for our senior workers who wish to continue working.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Yip Hon Weng has asked about how the Government can ensure that our senior workers can continue to contribute to the economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Over many years, we have put in place policies to support senior workers to continue to work for longer if they wish to do so, and build towards stronger retirement adequacy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As a result, our senior resident employment rate has remained healthy and even increased despite the recent economic turbulence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These wage offsets will be automatically disbursed to employers who qualify.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In response to Mr Desmond Choo's question, I am happy to announce that the Part-time Re-employment Grant (PTRG) will be extended to 2025.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This grant will increase the availability of part-time re-employment to senior workers in participating companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To receive up to $125,000 in grant support, employers have to offer part-time re-employment, implement flexible work arrangements (FWAs) at the workplace and adopt structured career planning for their mature and senior employees aged 45 and above.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This will help more senior workers to stay in employment, develop the skills needed to grow with the company, and extend their career longevity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Senior workers themselves, too, play a key role to make this process a success.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I encourage them to be open and proactive in embracing new opportunities, and ready to upskill and pivot to new job roles as they emerge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: (In English): I want to thank Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Heng Chee How, Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Mr Sharael Taha for their support for these efforts that will benefit senior workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Ms Jessica Tan also asked how many enterprises have taken up both schemes and the roles those senior workers took on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Senior Employment Credit (SEC) has in fact benefited almost 100,000 employers that hired over 461,000 senior workers since it was introduced.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: At the same time, more than 5,700 employers successfully applied for the Part-time Re-employment Grant (PTRG) and committed to implementing progressive senior employment policies, which we expect to benefit over 45,000 senior workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Employers from a wide variety of sectors have benefited from both schemes, such as wholesale and retail trade, accommodation and food service activities, and manufacturing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These employers offer a range of job roles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Leslie Basil Danker is one of our senior workers who has been with the renowned Raffles Hotel Singapore for 51 years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: He has been a beneficiary of the Part-time Re-employment Grant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Since starting out with the maintenance department in 1972, Mr Danker has taken on various event management roles and supervisory responsibilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Today, he is the mentor resident historian of Raffles Hotel, working on a part-time basis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This arrangement allowed him to wind down and spend more time with his family while continuing to share the hotel's rich history with guests through guided tours.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Perhaps some of you might be on his guided tour one of these days.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: His detailed knowledge of the hotel's roots came to the fore during the hotel's landmark restoration process from 2017 to 2019, where he worked closely with engineers, architects and interior designers for the undertaking of the renovation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is an excellent example of how the Part-time Re-employment Grant has benefited both the senior worker and the employer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Applications for the Part-time Re-employment Grant will reopen in April, which is next month.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I hope that employers will leverage the resources provided through these schemes to put in place progressive practices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Our tripartite partners have also been working with companies to improve senior workers' employability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: SNEF introduced a guidebook to help employers conduct structured career planning and NTUC is working with employers to adopt structured career planning through their Company Training Committees (CTCs).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Structured career planning provides employers with a process to proactively map out future business needs, identify skills that senior workers need to develop to grow with the company and support them in acquiring those skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This not only protects our senior workers' employability and extends their career longevity but also helps employers retain an experienced pool of workers amidst a tight labour market.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As Mr Abdul Samad, Mr Heng Chee How and Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman pointed out, retirement adequacy is another key area that we support senior workers on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For those between 55 and 65, we will press on ahead.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: A 55-year-old member today can expect monthly retirement payouts to be boosted by about 10%.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will also continue to support employers with the CPF Transition Offset.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I want to thank our tripartite partners for their support and consensus for this very important move.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These recommendations are necessary for senior workers who continue working to enter their retirement with more confidence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Chairman, we have put in place measures to uplift our platform workers and senior workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will need to work closely with stakeholders to implement the initiatives I have shared about and will count on support from fellow Singaporeans to mutually reinforce an inclusive and strengthened workforce where no one is left behind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Because as my sisters and brothers from the unions would say – every worker matters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Members who have contributed ideas on securing fairer and more inclusive workplaces.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Minister Tan See Leng spoke about journeying with you every step of the way.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: A fairer and more progressive workplace enables everyone, regardless of background, to contribute according to your strengths and interests and achieve your fullest potential.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I will share more on how we plan to continue journeying with you.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The pandemic has changed the way we work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Flexible work arrangements (FWAs) have become more prevalent and important.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Employers increasingly see the value of FWAs to attract and retain talent and to tap on a wider pool of manpower.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: While the focus during the pandemic was on telecommuting, FWAs go beyond telecommuting and include other work arrangements such as part-time work, staggered work hours, job sharing, flexible shift scheduling and so on.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As several Members such as Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Louis Ng, Miss Rachel Ong, Mr Sharael Taha and Ms Yeo Wan Ling highlighted, we can do more to support caregivers, seniors and persons with disabilities (PwDs) to continue working or to re-enter the workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: FWAs are a key strategy to do so.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We have made good progress and we will press on with tripartite partners to encourage more FWAs in a win-win manner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Businesses have different operating contexts and employees also have varied needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The key is for management and staff to have regular dialogue with each other to better understand each other's needs and build mutual trust.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Implementing FWAs in a rigid manner before employers are ready risks creating a more acrimonious workplace culture and affecting workplace productivity, which ultimately hurts employers and employees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: While we can understand Mr Louis Chua's and Mr Louis Ng's good intentions, legislation is not a panacea.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In jurisdictions with FWA legislation, employers can still reject requests that are not practicable for the business.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The UK, one of the first few countries that implemented a right to request FWAs legislation, only saw the proportion of UK workers using FWAs increasing very marginally from 26% in 2013 to 30% in 2020.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We need to first focus on shaping the right norms at work and building mutual understanding between employers and employees on FWAs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To Mr Gerald Giam's question, while employers have the prerogative to accept or reject an FWA request, they must have valid reasons for their decision.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: At the same time, employees should be reasonable in their requests and use FWAs responsibly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For example, certain forms of FWAs are simply not practical for some jobs, such as expecting full telecommuting for a job role in machine maintenance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Some FWAs may also have significant resource implications, which employers understandably need to take into consideration when assessing the request.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We must also differentiate the impact of FWAs on individual and team productivity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For instance, while some employees may feel more productive telecommuting and want to work from home more frequently, team productivity could fall due to reduced in-person interaction and collaboration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As such, we need to allow employers and employees time to adjust and find the optimal balance at the individual employee and business levels when implementing FWAs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: What we want to see is a workplace norm where employees feel comfortable requesting for FWAs and understanding that while not all requests can be acceded to due to business needs, the requests will be assessed properly and fairly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The tripartite partners will deliberate on these issues when crafting the Tripartite Guidelines, and we will consult widely, to ensure that the guidelines are practical and well-balanced in supporting the needs of both businesses as well as employees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Besides shaping norms, we have been working with the Tripartite Partners to strengthen support for employers in implementing FWAs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Many Members of Parliament have called for this over the years, including Ms Yeo Wan Ling, Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Louis Chua, Mr Louis Ng, Miss Rachel Ong, Mr Sharael Taha and Dr Wan Rizal, and many others.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: It is in employers' interest to make FWAs more available, as our surveys have found that FWAs had the greatest impact on staff retention amongst other progressive workplace policies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I encourage employers who offer FWAs to adopt the voluntary Tripartite Standard on Flexible Work Arrangements and be recognised as progressive employers on Workforce Singapore's MyCareersFuture Portal (MCF) and job fairs, so as to better attract jobseekers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Last year, the number of employees who worked in companies that adopted the Tripartite Standard increased by 18%.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In total, more than 29% of all employees now work in companies that have adopted the Tripartite Standard.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: One example of a progressive employer is Starbucks, which many of us are familiar with.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Starbucks Singapore offers a diverse range of FWAs, including part-time, flexi-shifts and shift swapping for their frontline employees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: They provide additional support to employees with needs, such as by allowing parents to switch to part-time work to spend more time with their children or new-born, or to care for their dependents or family members with special needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Employees doing office-based tasks are allowed to telecommute where possible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The flexibility and support accorded to employees, across different roles, has contributed to Starbucks' low attrition rate for their employees, as well as four out of five managerial posts being filled by their own in-house talent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I want to thank our tripartite partners – SNEF and NTUC – for their strong commitment in promoting FWAs at the workplace.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Just last year alone, the tripartite partners engaged around 2,000 employers, HR practitioners and employees to encourage the adoption of the Tripartite Standard on FWAs and implementation of flexible work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: These are done through SNEF's training engagements and NTUC's Better Workplace Campaign.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We also continue to see more employers tap on various resources such as IHRP's Playbook on Hybrid Workplaces and free clinics, and sector-specific guides offered by TAFEP.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will continue to develop more resources to guide employers on how to comply with the upcoming Guidelines.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Nevertheless, as we expect more people to take up FWAs, it will be increasingly important to ensure that HR practitioners are equipped to implement it in a fair manner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will continue to enhance these efforts to enable FWAs at the workplace.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: If done well, we can create family-friendly work environments for our caregivers, which many think will be more sustainable than legislating parent-care leave, as Mr Louis Ng suggested.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: After-hours communication, which Mr Melvin Yong raised, is another example of the importance of HR capabilities in the implementation of policies to ensure work flexibility is adopted appropriately.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To date, more than 500 company representatives have attended SNEF's workshops and briefings that help HR to implement this policy, which was actually derived from a template developed by the Alliance for Action on Work-Life Harmony.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Since the launch of the Tripartite Advisory on Mental Well-being at Workplaces in 2020, MOM and the Workplace Safety and Health Council have been encouraging companies to adopt the recommendations within the Tripartite Advisory that best suit their own company's needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: And as shared earlier, legislation such as the right-to-rest and the right-to-disconnect can create a rigid and litigious workplace culture.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Instead, we should adopt an enabling approach by encouraging employers to regularly engage employees to implement company policies that best suit both business and personal needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We agree with Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Sharael Taha and Ms Yeo Wan Ling that job redesign is important to enable FWAs at workplaces.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Companies requiring further support in job redesign to make their jobs more productive and attractive for workers, can tap on Government schemes, such as the Support for Job Redesign under the Productivity Solutions Grant.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Women in particular benefit from FWAs, as they often carry heavier caregiving responsibilities at home.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: There are also women who may take a break from their careers and need more support to return to work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Therefore, in June last year, Workforce Singapore (WSG) launched an initiative called herCareer. herCareer includes employment facilitation programmes and services that support women jobseekers, including walk-in interviews to meet with hiring employers on the spot.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Community partners can also play an important part in supporting women at work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For example, the Singapore Business Federation launched the Singapore Women Entrepreneurs Network in 2021, to nurture and support women talent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In the same year, the Singapore Council of Women's Organisations (SCWO) introduced a mentoring programme for aspiring women directors to help them achieve their professional development goals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: NTUC U Women and Family has further expanded its Women Supporting Women Mentorship Programme across the island, where women in the community are mentored by women leaders and union leaders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: NTUC U Women and Family, NTUC LearningHub and e2i also started a career returner programme called "Women Returning to Work", which includes training and job-matching opportunities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Concurrently, WSG collaborates with other community partners to support women returning to work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will continue to work with partners to provide women with the support they need, and we encourage employers to continue to do their part.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We recognise that some groups may need more support to achieve their full potential in the workforce, such as persons with disabilities (PwDs) and ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We are committed to providing them with the support they need, working hand-in-hand with our partners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We are encouraged that the employment rate of resident PwDs has continued to improve, reaching 31.4% in 2021 to 2022.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: But we can do better as a society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Miss Rachel Ong asked about raising the workforce participation rate of PwDs, while Mr Sharael Taha asked about creating more employment opportunities for them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Our whole of society needs to come together to achieve this aspirational goal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Under the Enabling Masterplan 2030, a new task force comprising members of the public, people and private sectors has been set up to develop new ways of supporting the employment of PwDs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: MOM will be enhancing the Enabling Employment Credit (EEC).

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Today, the EEC provides employers of PwDs earning below $4,000 a month with permanent wage offsets of up to 20%.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Employers who hire PwDs who have not been employed for at least six months receive an additional time-limited wage offset of up to 10% for six months.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This enhancement is on top of separate Government grants that provide employers with support to improve the workplace, redesign the job or provide training as needed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Ms Vivian Ser, a wife and mother, has been working with Novotel as a cook with support from the EEC and SG Enable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Novotel's HR team worked together with Ms Ser's job and mobility coaches during her onboarding process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As Ms Ser is visually impaired, she takes on parts of the kitchen process which do not involve heating, such as vacuum sealing and plating.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Novotel also put in place simple workplace accommodations, such as a talking scale and tactile stickers to help her navigate her environment safely.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Ms Ser's husband and son are her biggest cheerleaders and also provide practical support such as in her transport arrangements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: With support from her family, employer, colleagues and coaches, Ms Ser recently reached her one-year anniversary with Novotel.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As seen from Ms Ser's story, holistic support makes a difference to helping persons with disabilities enter and stay in employment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Gerald Giam asked what can be done to address discrimination associated with disabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: A first step that we can all take is to avoid stereotyping and to recognise that everyone has skills and experience which they can bring to our teams at work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Looking ahead, the Tripartite Committee on Workplace Fairness has recommended that the proposed Workplace Fairness legislation protect PwDs against workplace discrimination.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Miss Rachel Ong also asked about retirement adequacy for PwDs and their caregivers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Eligible lower-income workers, including PwDs and their caregivers, receive the Workfare Income Supplement (WIS), which will boost their income and retirement savings through cash payments and CPF contributions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We have further enhanced Workfare from January 2023 to allow all eligible PwDs to qualify for the highest pay-out tier, regardless of age.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This will provide up to $4,200 in annual payments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Government also provides additional support to boost retirement adequacy, which would support PwDs and their caregivers if they are unable to work and have little retirement savings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This includes the Silver Support scheme, which provides quarterly cash payouts of up to $900 to seniors who had low or no incomes during their working years and have little family support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To encourage top-ups, we also introduced the Matched Retirement Savings Scheme (MRSS) in 2021.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Under the MRSS, the Government will match top-ups of up to $600 per year to eligible seniors' CPF accounts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: These measures will also help boost the retirement adequacy of homemakers whom Mr Saktiandi spoke about.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Miss Rachel Ong asked about support for caregivers of PwDs who wish to return to the workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Caregivers can tap on Workforce Singapore's suite of employment facilitation programmes and services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For example, caregivers who need job search assistance can visit WSG's Careers Connect and NTUC's e2i career centres for career advisory and guidance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Those who need a skills top-up can apply for Career Conversion Programmes (CCPs), which provide training and salary support to employers who hire and reskill mid-career jobseekers for new occupations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Another group that we pay close attention to is ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Employment is critical for their successful reintegration into society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Ex-offenders sometimes face challenges, such as stigmatisation and limited career opportunities, upon their release.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The problems can be compounded by low educational qualifications, lack of industry-relevant skills and recent work experience.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The challenges are more acute in the initial years after release, as ex-offenders face problems transiting from prison to the work environment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: A hiring incentive for ex-offenders will help encourage a wider range of employers to provide job opportunities to ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will introduce a new hiring incentive, the Uplifting Employment Credit (UEC) to continue supporting the hiring of ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Under the new UEC, employers who hire ex-offenders through Yellow Ribbon Singapore and Singapore Prison Service's employment programmes will automatically qualify for a wage offset of 20% for the first nine months, amounting to up to $5,400 for each ex-offender employee.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Employers who hire eligible ex-offenders directly can apply through IRAS to receive this credit.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We hope that this will go some way in supporting the employment of ex-offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Chairman, let me say a few words in Mandarin.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: (In Mandarin):   To build an inclusive society, we will help everyone in society to achieve their full potential in the workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will also introduce a new hiring incentive to help ex-offenders where the employers who hire ex-offenders will receive monthly wage offsets of up to 20% for a duration of nine months, amounting up to $5,400 for each newly-hired ex-offender employee.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Together, with the support of employers, community partners and the Government, we can help PwDs with disabilities and ex-offenders contribute to our workforce and society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: (In English): Mr Chairman, everyone must play their part to secure fairer and more inclusive workplaces for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Government will continue to provide the support that you need and journey with you every step of the way.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Deputy Chairman, I would like to make two clarifications with respect to the first segment of my speech.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Senior Minister of State Koh, Senior Minister of State Zaqy, Minister of State Gan and I have shared about the Ministry of Manpower (MOM)'s three themes for this Committee of Supply (COS): (a) seizing opportunities, (b) strengthening support for you and (c) securing better workplaces with you.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I have earlier covered the first two themes and I will now touch on the third – how we stand in solidarity to secure safer, fairer and more progressive workplaces with you.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are doing so in a couple of ways.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Minister of State Gan has shared details on our efforts to support our women at work and help persons with disabilities (PwDs) and ex-offenders find employment.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Senior Minister of State Zaqy has also elaborated on our efforts to ensure safety in the workplace.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members will have seen the 20 interim recommendations by the Tripartite Committee on Workplace Fairness, which I co-chair with Brothers Ng Chee Meng and Dr Robert Yap.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Calls for legislation date back to 1998, with various parties, including Labour Members, proposing for legislation to strengthen our efforts in tackling discrimination.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Indeed, this significant move is going to strengthen our overall framework to uphold workplace fairness.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Gerald Giam asked for comprehensive protection for PwDs, while Mr Leong Mun Wai suggested to cover sexual orientation in the legislation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: They both can be assured that all forms of discrimination are not tolerated.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is our national policy and it is reflected in the Tripartite Guidelines for Fair Employment Practices (TGFEP) today.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Stronger protection against discrimination in the proposed areas also supports Singapore's key social and economic objectives.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For instance, protecting against discrimination on the grounds of age helps to support the employment of mature workers, which is critical for our ageing society.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These characteristics are the common and familiar forms of workplace discrimination in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have experienced dealing with these cases and we are confident to mediate them effectively.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Tripartite partners will work with relevant stakeholders to ensure that there is clarity on issues, such as definitions and scope of employers' responsibilities to enable the legislation to achieve its intended effect.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Some Members have raised suggestions on the legislation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Leong asked how the legislation will address job security for Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Legislation will benefit Singaporeans by better protecting them against workplace discrimination.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There will be a wider range of enforcement levers against errant employers that are more effective as deterrence against workplace discrimination.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Fair Consideration Framework job advertising requirement will also be legislated, which will allow us to take action against employers who breach this requirement, using the new enforcement levers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Tripartite Committee has also recommended protection against retaliation for those who report workplace discrimination or harassment, to give assurance to employees to come forward to report it.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The majority of complaints on nationality discriminations are by locals indeed.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, they will benefit from the greater protection.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Leong also suggested small firms should not be exempted from the legislation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Small firms may not have the corporate competencies to comprehensively implement the new rules from day one.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As the proposed legislation is only the first step, we will exempt small firms with fewer than 25 employees for a start.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Workers in small firms, however, will continue to still be covered by TGFEP.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Those who are unfairly dismissed can lodge claims with the Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management (TADM).

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For these employers, we will also step up education and enforcement efforts via TGFEP.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Tripartite Committee agrees that we will monitor the ground situation after legislation is introduced and review the exemption with a view to tightening it within five years.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Leong referred to a specific case in a religious organisation in 2013.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For that case, based on prevailing guidelines and laws, the church did not have sufficient grounds to dismiss the employee.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With the introduction of the Workplace Fairness Legislation, the Tripartite Committee consulted various agencies, religious organisations and advocacy groups on their views.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We recognise that maintaining religious harmony is important in our multi-religious society.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is, therefore, important to give religious organisations the space to practise their religion.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On the question of vaccination-differentiated safe management measures (VDS), we have reached out to and offered employment assistance to the unvaccinated workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: They can also approach Workforce Singapore (WSG) or Employment and Employability Institute (e2i), if they require further assistance.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Workers who feel that their employers are imposing vaccination as a requirement without genuine occupational needs may approach MOM or TAFEP for assistance.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Since the release of the updated advisory on COVID-19 vaccination at the workplace in October 2022, there has only been a handful of such complaints.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Janet Ang and Ms Yeo Wan Ling will also be assured to know that we will continue to engage employers, employees, HR partners and other key stakeholders to make clear the intent of the legislation and the whole-of-society effort required to uphold workplace fairness.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: During the implementation process, we will also work with NTUC to help employees to better navigate the case management process and seek remedies for their grievances.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And we will work with SNEF to guide employers to adopt Fair Employment practices and comply with the legislation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Even as we introduce stronger worker protections in legislation, and let me emphasise this, we want to preserve Singapore's harmonious and non-litigious workplace culture.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To this end, the committee has also made recommendations to encourage disputes to be resolved within the firm in the first instance.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And if not, through mediation to repair the employment relationship where possible, with adjudication at the Courts only as a last resort.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will continue to welcome all feedback, including from Members today.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Tripartite Committee will take the feedback into consideration for its final recommendations.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With that, Mr Chairman, let me now conclude in Mandarin.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: (In Mandarin):   In the past year, I have been involved in many dialogue sessions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Most Singaporeans understand that we face many challenges on our road to economic recovery.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I am glad that Singaporeans are still hopeful about their future and actively sharing their hopes and aspirations with us.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This reminds me of a Xinyao song, "Small Stream that Flows Forever".

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The lyrics say “who does not dream when they are young”.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Back when I first entered the workforce, I was just as ambitious, but I understood that my career path may not be smooth, and I may face various obstacles before arriving at my intended destination.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Whether you are a young person, or like me, a middle-aged person, rest assured that we will journey with you every step of the way, and help you become more resilient and move forward with you.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Whether you are in your early-20s, 30s, mid-40s or late-50s, we will empower you to find and work towards new opportunities and seize better job opportunities.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If you are looking for a career change, you can be assured of the support we will provide you to upskill and re-skill.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If you have just lost your job, you can be assured that we will step in to help you in your job search.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If your interest is in hands-on work, you can be assured of more opportunities to learn.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will help you in your career transition.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If you are approaching retirement, we will continue to strengthen the CPF system, help you meet basic retirement needs, so that you can enjoy your golden years.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As the saying goes, prevention is better than cure.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Whether Singaporeans can continue to seize opportunities depends on their career health.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We should be responsible for our own career health, understand the needs of our career, industry trends, our interests and capabilities.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The feature will harness data analytics and artificial intelligence to provide you with more personalised jobs and skills insights to improve job matching.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We also need to build a more inclusive labour market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As the saying goes, "Every Trade has its Master".

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Even though "head" work remains a priority, we should not overlook "hands-on" work.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Regardless of the industry, there should be multiple pathways to success.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are looking into how we can redesign such jobs – with better starting salaries, better upskilling opportunities, and other ways to attract and retain workers in these jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Shifting society's perceptions of such jobs takes time and process, so we have to persevere.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are also strengthening support for Singaporeans' retirement adequacy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The CPF system is a key pillar for Singapore's retirement adequacy, and it meets workers' basic retirement needs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To ensure the CPF system remains relevant, we must study how we can boost the CPF monthly payouts for seniors.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the end of the song "Small Stream That Flows Forever", the lyrics say, "There are thousands of ups and downs in life, only the best confidantes meet forever, for their friendship is forever, like water flowing from its source".

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope you will see MOM as a close partner in your career path, provide feedback and suggestions and co-create and improve policies together.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is also the objective of the Government's Forward Singapore exercise to renew the social compact.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will continue to work with you to ride out the storm and move towards a better future!

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: It is very reassuring that our senior workers' employment rate is comparable to the OECD countries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Would it be useful to have a target employment rate for these senior workers?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: What measures beyond the Senior Employment Credit (SEC) and Part-time Re-employment Grant (PTRG) are needed to have more employers to hire senior workers?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Mr Desmond Choo for the question.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As he mentioned and as I shared in my speech earlier, we do have quite a good employment rate for our senior workers compared to OECD countries and other advanced Asian economies.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is with the background that we are really not doing too badly compared to other advanced economies.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: That again also helps to protect them and allows their aspirations to be realised.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And then some of these other measures, whether it is the Senior Employment Credit (SEC), whether it is the Part-Time Re-employment Grant (PTRG) that helps to reduce friction if employers feel that cost may be a consideration, we want to take away as many of those worries as possible from the employer side, to give them an extra leg-up to be able to get employment opportunities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But ultimately, what is important is to make sure our senior workers continue to upskill themselves.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: They must ultimately have the skills that the industry needs in order to be able to access employment opportunities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, it is a whole suite of efforts that we do from all angles and some of the things that we are doing with the tripartite partners are also going to be helpful, helping them to do structured career planning, making employers and HR professionals attuned to the need to look at job redesign.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Having a conversation with the workers before they reach retirement age in their 40s and 50s to start planning for the next step of their career so that even as they enter their 50s and 60s, they understand what the company wants and there is a concerted effort from the employer, the HR side as well as the workers to develop skills that are relevant to the company's longer-term objectives.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, it is a whole suite of efforts and I think at this moment we are all moving in the correct direction.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Let us continue to push on with what we are doing now and, hopefully, with the trajectory that we are seeing, the senior employment rate will continue to hit even higher levels in the next few years to come.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And as I said before in my speech, despite the pandemic and economic crisis, our senior employment rate has actually gone up and not declined.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, that is something encouraging that we want to pursue.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Will the Ministry also publish a SOL for skilled trades, industrial jobs and other essential occupations?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: For example, the UK's SOL includes welders, care workers for seniors, day care managers and healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: These are also occupations which are in such short supply in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: So, MOM can then use this to work with the industry and educational institutions to close the skills gaps, in our local workforce.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: The second question I have is that I note that Minister said that the SOL will be refreshed every three years.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I am not sure if this is sufficient, given the fast-evolving job market.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Could MOM update the SOL more frequently to ensure it stays relevant with the constantly evolving job market and circumstances?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, to that extent, I would rather keep the list to a very tight, narrow scope where we work very closely with the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI), the Ministry of National Development (MND), the Ministry of Health (MOH), and the different sectoral agencies to curate it and work through these agencies to address some of these sectors' shortages.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To the Member's second point about a three-yearly review, we also want to provide a certain level of certainty and predictability to businesses setting up here or businesses that are already operating here.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If we keep moving this list very frequently, businesses will find it very hard to adapt, to respond and to be nimble.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And I have already shared in my earlier speech what are some of the criteria that we will put in place.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I have one clarification for the Minister in regard to the CPF LIFE Escalation Plan.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: It is in regard to my concern that with the rising prices and inflation and, of course, my concern about the longer-term equilibrium inflation outlook that Singapore and countries globally are facing, how will seniors be affected?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: As of now, the CPF LIFE Escalating Plan rises by about 2% payouts annually.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, my suggestion in my Budget debate speech was whether it can be increased by another 50 basis points or possibly another 100 basis points, to take into consideration the rising prices for the current cohort and probably future cohorts, as an option beyond the 2% option that we have now; so as an additional option or a revision to the current 2%.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The CPF LIFE Escalating Plan has a lower start but over time, it actually exceeds the Standard and the Basic Plan, as we speak today.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Today, we are in an era where inflation is high because of the geopolitical uncertainties.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have also seen the global supply chain disruptions as well as a lot of interest rates tightening.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The broad initiatives, the broad measures that we put up today, will improve retirement adequacy over the medium to long term.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: During times of shocks such as what we have gone through the last two years and what we are still going through, the Government has constantly come in and intervened.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have had the Assurance Package; the GST Vouchers have become a permanent GST Voucher scheme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And there was a whole slew of support schemes that has been put up to support all Singaporeans and our CPF members to tide through this particular period.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: You can see the MOM schemes in terms of CPF financial retirement adequacy, as a long haul, over a very long period of time, to provide the basic retirement adequacy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And at certain times, if I may borrow a term, it is like an immunisation, you get a booster coming in from the Government to help to uplift the members' retirement lifestyle and smoothen out some of the expenses.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If you look at the measures that we have rolled out over the last 12 months or so, for the low-income, the coverage is very substantial and it covers practically all of the inflationary increases in terms of spending.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: First is, will the new workplace fairness legislation cover platform workers?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: And secondly, the Minister gave us the proportion of CPF members who meet the Basic Retirement Sum just now.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Can the Minister also tell us the proportion who can meet the Full Retirement Sum?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To the first clarification, the answer is yes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For the second clarification, in terms of the Full Retirement Sum, if you can let one or two other clarifications go through, I will come back to you.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Chairman, I would like to reiterate that there are about 260,000 women of economic age not in the workforce today.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: They will be a formidable workforce tapped for Singapore should we create the right conditions for our women to return to work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: I like to thank Minister of State Gan for acknowledging the work that the Labour Movement and the NTUC Women and Family Unit has done.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: I would, in addition, like to ask the Senior Minister of State how can the Government further the partnership with the Labour Movement to support women who are seeking employment?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Also, beyond the Enabling Employment Credit (EEC), what other employment support is there for persons with disabilities (PwDs)?

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The Government has been working in close partnership with NTUC and the unions to support women employment.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Looking forward, we think that there are more opportunities for the Government to work with the unions, especially the women union leaders, to form mentorship circles to expand our partnership with other women's groups and like-minded groups, to cast our net wider to be able to reach out to more women.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: As for support for persons with disabilities (PwDs), there is an Enabling Masterplan 2030.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: There is also a separate task force that has been formed.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: I believe MSF will also be sharing the details when ready.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I have three questions for the Minister, but before that, I would like to thank the Minister for answering all my questions except one with very direct and succinct answers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: First, the question that the Minister did not answer me.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Looking at the materials that were distributed by the Minister, the lower-income worker will get that by 2028, but that is far too long – five years to wait – bearing in mind that many of these workers also suffered considerably during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The last question, does the Minister expect Singaporeans to occupy a larger share of our IT jobs going forward, especially in higher positions, in the next five years, given that the number of IT graduates – local IT graduates – will be increasing significantly over the next few years?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: After all, you are from the same party.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On the second part of her clarification, let me set the entire context by giving the full response.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To the Member's first point, I wish to make an amendment that was on the Member's part about whether platform workers are covered by the workplace legislation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Workplace Fairness Legislation needs to have a formal contract – a formal relationship between the employer and the employee.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think the nature of platform work is that many of the platform workers have multiple platforms that they work for.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: You could be on one, you could also be on another.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think some of them have about two or three.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Perhaps Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon will be better placed to respond to this because of his deeper knowledge.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To Mr Leong's four points, thank you for that compliment.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is really the collective work of all of my colleagues in the Ministry of Manpower (MOM).

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I have also learnt a lot from my learned colleagues here in their responses and replies to your questions as well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If you look at it, we are at almost full employment.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At a point in time when our resident employment is at this kind of high level, for companies to want to grow, to fulfil all this and so on, they have to hire.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Obviously, in the fourth quarter, you see more non-residents finding jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To the Member's point about how certain I am that Singaporean PMEs are not disadvantaged because for the Employment Pass (EP) holders, the employers do not have to contribute to CPF, please refer to my numerous explanations in the past.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The way we calculate the Minimum Qualifying Salary is after taking into consideration the gross salary of a local – in a similar cohort – plus the CPF contribution of the employer and we set that as the benchmark.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If you look at it from the perspective of someone who has been here for 10 years, the salary of that EP holder is on a rising scale.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For the EP holder, for him to be able to get the EP, the company will have to set that qualifying salary probably at above $10,000.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With that, we believe that we have adequately addressed any form of income disparity between our locals and foreigners.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On top of that, we do not see a need for us to ensure that foreigners have to contribute to CPF because our CPF provides for retirement adequacy, housing – a roof over the heads of our Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We do not see the need to provide the same level of safety net for foreigners.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Hence, we do not impose this CPF contribution on them.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To the Member's point about how to accelerate the income under PWM, I will leave it to Senior Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad to answer the question.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Member's last point was about how I ensure that the larger share of IT jobs in high positions will go to Singaporeans in the next five years.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will continue, through all of the programmes that I have been painstakingly elaborating on over the last two days – whether it is SGEP, Global Ready Talent, Tech@SG – these are all programmes that we set up to train, to invest, to upskill and to reskill our Singaporean Core talent and we will continue to do so.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If Mr Leong has even more constructive programmes that we can do to train and upskill our Singaporean Core, I am happy to also take that into consideration.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But as to whether I can provide some form of guarantee over the next five years, whether they will all end up in high positions, I do not think anyone can guarantee that.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We can guarantee a level playing field at the outset at every single level, but I do not think anyone can guarantee a similar high outcome or success for everyone.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I just want to bring Members back to this infographic that we shared, which Mr Leong shared, which I thought was really quite clear.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Actually, most of your PWMs that Members see here are pretty much above $1,800.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The kind of wage growth is quite significant at 56%.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, there is a scheduled step, but at the same time, it can almost be guaranteed that almost all of them, in fact, all of them will exceed $1,800 at the start.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Let us not forget that the Government's approach goes beyond just wages too, if the Member forgot to include Workfare.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: If you think about $4,200 a year, that is about $350 per month, in addition, depending on your age and criteria, but generally, you could get as much as that.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: That covers about 25% of your wage in addition to top-ups by the Government.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, if you look at total income, I think, let us look at the entirety.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But I have to credit the unions as well as the employers for standing with us on this because the last two years have not been easy.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We have just come out of the pandemic and yet, to see both the Labour Movement and the employers agree to such aggressive pay increases, I think that speaks volumes of our tripartite movement in terms of supporting our lower-wage workers and standing in solidarity with them.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think it is quite critical for us to remember that we are still coming out of the pandemic and yet now we are agreeing to wage increases of 56% and 84% which are significant numbers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To push any further, I do not think the employers can take it.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, we have to keep watch, that is why the Government also supports them through the Progressive Wage Credit Scheme (PWCS).

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, I just thought to set the context.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But rest assured, we are all on the same page.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We are here to support our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The answer is no, because workplace fairness legislation only covers employer-employee relationships.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I did spend a significant part of my speech earlier to say why we are not classifying platform workers as employees – to maintain the flexibility that both parties desire.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But having said that, as I said in my speech before, the Tripartite Guidelines for Fair Employment Practices will scope in a clearer statement to say that any discrimination, even of contracted workers, will be deemed to be in violation of the Tripartite Guidelines for Fair Employment Practices.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: MOM can investigate and impose administrative penalties on these platform companies if they do discriminate.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
