text: The other thing which I hope perhaps Members will realise is that it is not in the interest of the companies to discriminate against workers who opt in for CPF simply because the scheme we are trying to propose here is that by 2024, those who are below 30 years old will be mandatorily required to contribute to CPF.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Which means that henceforth, as a cohort, all younger workers born after 1995, whichever timepoint they choose to enter platform work – by the time, they are 40 years old or 50 years old – so long as they are born after 1995, platform companies will need to contribute CPF for them.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In other words, over time, the bulk of the workers available for platform work will need mandatory CPF.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Therefore, it is not in the company's interest to disadvantage those in this larger group of workforce that will then constrain their ability to get labour.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Leong, we will circle back to you.

speaker: The Chairman
text: There are three Members that have yet to ask clarifications.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I appreciate the Minister of State shared that we are not ready to legislate parent care leave yet, but can I at least ask that we consider tripartite standards or tripartite guidelines on paid parent care leave?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Second, could I ask what are the reasons as to why the Government provides parent care leave to public servants and how those reasons do not apply to all other workers?

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Well, I would like to reiterate that the Government recognises that caregiving for parents is an important responsibility, especially with Singapore's ageing population.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: But beyond legislation, which the hon Member Louis Ng has suggested, it is useful for us to take a step back and ask ourselves, for caregivers, especially of elderly parents, what would be more sustainable support for them.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Would just one or two more days of parent care leave make a lot of difference?

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Or is it something that is more sustainable in the form of family-friendly workplace culture that would be more useful for these caregivers?

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The Government encourages employers to have family-friendly practices and the Public Service leads by example by providing the parent care leave for our own employees.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We hope that other employers out there will do likewise: care for their employees, have family-friendly practices and provide the flexibility that the employees need to care for their elderly family members.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The Government also has strengthened other areas of support for caregivers of seniors, including those who have to juggle between work and caregiving.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Caregivers can tap on a range of care services, such as home- and day-care to support the day and social needs of their elderly loved ones.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: There are also various respite care options in senior care centres and nursing homes to help caregivers to look after their seniors for short periods of time, including over the weekends.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: So, we do look at a more holistic set of support for caregivers of the elderly, and not just pin on a few more days of parent care leave.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: I feel that this will really support HR professionals in their expanded role.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: I also note that he mentioned the Institute for Human Resource Professionals (IHRP) has certification and playbooks.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: He also mentioned that IHRP has skills badges for HR professionals.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think they are very useful, and especially one that, I hope, the HR community appreciates in terms of the development that we have put in.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I will start off with the skills badges.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It could be HR professionals with skills in various competencies such as talent management and strategic workforce planning.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: As the appointed Skills Development Partner for HR, IHRP will work with the industry to identify new skills gaps and will continue to refresh the skills badges to keep up with the emerging trends.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: To the Member's second question in terms of the work that we do with playbooks and HR certifications, the Job Transformation Maps (JTMs) developed together with the industries support employers and HR in their job transformation efforts.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And that is something that we think will value-add to our HR community.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Each of the JTM provides detailed insights on the impact of technology and automation on the industry and the workforce, as well as lays out pathways for employers to transform jobs and give opportunities to workers to acquire the requisite skills.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is important because you want to help to point out to the companies what the resources are that are relevant to their job design needs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This, I hope, will help the HR community to work towards the redesigning of jobs, as well as help them through digital transformation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This, I think, remains a key enabler towards sustaining business transformation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I also encourage, especially for digital transformation, the HR community to tap on IMDA's CTO-as-a-Service scheme, the HR Tech Transformation scheme, as well as the Productivity Solutions Grant.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, there are various Government grants that are available to support our HR community.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I hope that they find these useful and work towards career transformation for the businesses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: I wish to ask the Ministry, given the current high inflation environment, whether it is a good time now to increase the CPF contribution rate for senior workers, as this will add to business costs for companies?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And we are doing this at an early time to give employers ample notice so that they can adjust and manage the impact on business costs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, the offset will certainly help in this current tranche of increase that we are planning to do.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: All these offsets that we give for the increase in CPF contribution rate is on top of all the other schemes that we have been giving to support employment of older workers, like the Senior Employment Credit (SEC) and the Part-time Re-employment Grant (PTRG).

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: All these will help to ameliorate the cost impact on any older workers that the company employs.

speaker: The Chairman
text: So, I will take the last two clarifications.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai and Ms Yeo Wan Ling.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Just a further clarification from my question just now.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But I think he has not compared like to like.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What the PSP has recommended in terms of the living wage is $1,800 take-home pay, but the figure shown in the material is actually gross salary.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I would also want to ask one more clarification question with the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If the Government is already contributing more in terms of Workfare Income Supplement (WIS), why do we not just add the WIS into the salary and then make it a clear one-policy living wage?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: There is one other question I want to clarify with the Minister.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Of course, Minister, I have got that answer from you before.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But I think we have not exhausted the discussion, so let me carry on with that.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I am afraid, Mr Leong, it is not time for discussion.

speaker: The Chairman
text: And this is your second bite of the cherry.

speaker: The Chairman
text: So, I would ask you to keep it concise and short, please.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, can I ask about the salary component that you have talked about, that you have adjusted the salary for Employment Passes (EPs) so that it is comparable with Singaporeans having to pay CPF contributions, while the EP holders do not have to pay CPF contributions?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Do you think that is a strong enough deterrent, really?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Or do you think that the recommendation made by us, that of imposing a levy, would be a better solution?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I am not sure how much more I have to go through the sheet.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But we already have a schedule and every single one of these items here will be past $1,800 for sure.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I do not know how you want to define your living wage, but anyone can put a number.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Or like what I have said, what is different between our approach and what you said – anyone can put a number.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Be it $1,800, $1,600, or $2,500; just name it.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But the difference is that, in our approach, the employers and the Labour Movement have come to a consensus.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Basically, it means that when we put a number down here, it is something that employers say they can bear; the market can absorb.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And the wage growths here are already as aggressive as I think anyone can do during the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: You have to be very fair to employers in the market.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I just want to say this again – bear in mind the market conditions in which we operate.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: At the same time our approach is one that I think is fair and balanced, one that the market is prepared to pay; the employers have all agreed to this.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Therefore, to a large extent, I think it is bearable to the market and supported by the Government.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Whether you put Workfare into this or not, honestly, what really matters to the workers is what they get in their pockets every month.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: That is where we have to put it in place various measures.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is not the only measure because the Government also provides other schemes, including ComCare, Silver Support and the whole slew of Government grants that go into our workforce to support our lower-wage workers, including healthcare subsidies, housing subsidies and education subsidies.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, the Government puts a lot of commitment and that is where, I think, we show how we care overall, not just in terms of living wage, but every other support and subsidy you can think of, the Government can provide.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: But I think what is key is whether you can deliver and you can execute.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: That is where our focus will be in the next coming years.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Leong, I think in the interest of time, I will try and keep it short.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But, actually, all I can do is just refer you back to the Hansard reports for you to read the thing.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: You have asked quite a number of questions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I just want to address some of it.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I have been in the private sector all my life and I have also set up businesses in many countries.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think if you do that, many of my old networks will probably give this place a miss.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The reality is that if you structure an industry, if you want to grow the industry, it is a combination of making sure that we invest in our people and, at the same time, we are also able to imbibe – the word is "imbibe", not "open the doors and let them in freely".

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To imbibe enough talent so that they can actually complement our local talent and we all then prosper together.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We also still ensure that these companies can get the additional talent they need – which you see is the common and recurring theme around our debates for the last many days.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There are many, many Members on both sides of the House who keep telling us and lamenting how tight the talent and the manpower situation is in this country.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, we want to ensure that these companies still have access to high-quality complementary candidates so that when there are certain niche skills and skills that continue to evolve, we can bring them in and also train our local talent as well to create more good job opportunities for our locals.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If you look at it, employers do not have infinite budgets for manpower.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We should think about a win-win partnership where we benefit, we let the employer win, so that Singaporean employees will also have that win.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: That is why in all of our policies, we focus on making sure that our economy is vibrant so that there are enough resources for us to continue to invest back in our people to continue to develop Singapore, progress Singapore to a place that is brimming with opportunities, hope, and always, with optimism.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope that you can put that aside and focus on bringing all of us together and building that Singapore for our future.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Because I think that is the core of what we do.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I am afraid, Ms Yeo, we have hit our 6.15 pm guillotine time, so you cannot ask your second clarification.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I am afraid, Mr Leong, we have reached the guillotine time.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Desmond Choo, would you like to take leave to withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: Mr Chairman I would like to thank Minister Tan See Leng, Senior Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad, Dr Koh Poh Koon and Minister of State Gan Siow Huang for their indulgence in answering all our cuts to the best of their abilities and time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: We know that it is difficult to keep the workforce competitive in the midst of difficult structural problems, like ageing population and geopolitical tensions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: I hope that I have appropriate lyrics to a Chinese song to the thank him, but I do not.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: I can only offer him our appreciation that it is very reassuring that MOM and himself, will accompany the Singapore population through when they first get the first job to when they retire.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: With this, I beg leave to withdraw my amendment.
